title: MESA: An Evaluation Framework for Compositional, Semantic, and Spatial Generalization in Robotics
abstract: Despite growing interest in foundation models for robotic manipulation, systematic evaluation of their capabilities remains elusive. Existing benchmarks are either narrow and saturated, offering little signal on SOTA methods, broadly scoped, providing diversity at the cost of controlled experimentation, or require training on large, messy open-source datasets. We introduce MESA, an evaluation framework designed for precise, reproducible measurement of language-conditioned policy generalization. MESA provides five evaluation suites that isolate in-distribution performance and four distinct axes of generalization: spatial configuration, object instance, object category, and subtask composition, enabling researchers to diagnose where and why policies fail, not just whether they fail. To populate these suites at scale, we develop MESA-Gen, a pipeline for task and demonstration generation built by improving MimicGen. We instantiate the framework on two platforms and release both: the single-arm MESA suite, and BiMESA, the first large-scale benchmark for bimanual generalization. We evaluate seven baseline methods spanning diffusion policies, VLM-based approaches, and pretrained VLAs, finding that the strongest model achieves only 52% on MESA and 49% on BiMESA, providing meaningful signal while leaving ample room for progress. MESA rankings are broadly consistent with RoboArena scores, suggesting that MESA captures method-level differences relevant beyond simulation. Project website: https://pairlab.github.io/MESA.

title: MEC: Machine-Learning-Assisted Generalized Entropy Calibration for Semi-Supervised Mean Estimation
abstract: Obtaining high-quality labels is costly, whereas unlabeled covariates are often abundant, motivating semi-supervised inference methods with reliable uncertainty quantification. Prediction-powered inference (PPI) leverages a machine-learning predictor trained on a small labeled sample to improve efficiency, but it can lose efficiency under model misspecification and suffer from coverage distortions due to label reuse. We introduce Machine‑Learning‑Assisted Generalized Entropy Calibration (MEC), a cross‑fitted, calibration‑weighted variant of PPI. MEC improves efficiency by reweighting labeled samples to better align with the target population, using a principled calibration framework based on Bregman projections. This yields robustness to affine transformations of the predictor and relaxes requirements for validity by replacing conditions on raw prediction error with weaker projection‑error conditions. As a result, MEC attains the semiparametric efficiency bound under weaker assumptions than existing PPI variants. Across simulations and a real‑data application, MEC achieves near‑nominal coverage and tighter confidence intervals than CF‑PPI and vanilla PPI.

title: LungMend: A Healthy-Only Latent Diffusion Shape Prior for Lung Mask Correction in Severe Tuberculosis CT
abstract: Lung segmentation models such as R231 are widely used, but they fail on severe tuberculosis (TB) CT: cavities and consolidations look like non-lung tissue and are left out of the mask. We present LungMend, a post-processing model that corrects such masks using only healthy anatomy. A latent diffusion model, trained on healthy lungs with synthetically corrupted masks, learns to recover the complete lung from the faulty mask and the bone anatomy, without any pathological data or CT intensities. LungMend recovers cavities and consolidations that R231 misses and improves accuracy on expert-annotated slices. Code: https://github.com/noureddinekhiati/LungMend

title: Low-Rank Clebsch--Gordan Coupling for Equivariant Spherical Forecasting
abstract: Spherical-harmonic neural operators provide an efficient representation for global forecasting, but their discretized pointwise nonlinearities can break rotational equivariance through aliasing. Clebsch-Gordan (CG) tensor products provide exactly equivariant interactions between spherical-harmonic representations, but their computational cost grows rapidly with spectral bandwidth and has limited their use at forecasting scale. We introduce LCG-SFNO, which combines low-rank CG interactions within a controlled low-degree band with coefficient-space residual propagation and an exactly projected quadratic nonlinearity, preserving SO(3) equivariance throughout the learned operator. To make the CG interaction practical, we further develop SSHCG, a sparse GPU implementation with a factorized alternative for wider coupled bands. On spherical shallow-water dynamics and the ERA5-based WeatherBench benchmark, LCG-SFNO reduces rotational error to numerical precision (more than three orders of magnitude below SFNO on shallow water and five orders of magnitude below it on WeatherBench), while matching SFNO on shallow-water forecasting and substantially improving forecast skill relative to SFNO on WeatherBench. Matched ablations show that CG coupling accelerates convergence, while SSHCG keeps the coupling to about 10 percent of a training step at the operating bandwidth, making exact equivariant coupling practical at forecasting scale.

title: LiveFigure: Generating Editable Scientific Illustration with VLM Agents
abstract: Scientific illustrations are essential for depicting conceptual designs, methodologies, and experimental workflows in research, playing a pivotal role in communicating complex academic insights. However, creating high-quality scientific illustrations remains a labor-intensive task for human scientists. While recent generative image models have advanced prompt-based editing, the synthesis of fully **editable** figures remains a fundamental challenge. Valid editability involves structured transformations of graphical elements, scales, attributes, and text, rather than simple pixel-level changes. Existing models generate raster outputs that do not support manual correction or layout adjustment, limiting their utility in scientific publishing, where editable vector figures are typically required for submission. To address this challenge, we introduce **LiveFigure**, an agentic framework driven by VLM agents that imitates the multi-step drawing workflow of human researchers. It first plans figure blueprints by drawing inspiration from high-quality references in previous works, then generates executable scripts that produce figures via the PowerPoint interface based on skills and experience, and finally refines the outputs with targeted visual diagnostics, producing fully vectorized, editable figures that meet publication standards. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LiveFigure generates inherently editable figures, achieving 80% publication-readiness in only 17 manual edits, far surpassing the 24% rate of the strongest baseline, NanoBanana. Human preference studies further validate this advantage, with LiveFigure securing a 60% win rate against NanoBanana. Our code is available at [https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/LiveFigure.git](https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/LiveFigure.git).

title: LithoDreamer: A Physics-Informed World Model for Multi-Stage Computational Lithography
abstract: As semiconductor technology nodes scale, computational lithography is essential for ensuring yield and performance. However, lithography is a continuous physical process involving mask optimization, optical imaging, resist exposure, and development, which existing models fail to capture. To overcome this limitation, we present LithoDreamer, the first physics-informed World Model (WM) framework for computational lithography, which formulates the ''Layout-Mask-Resist Image-After Development Image (ADI)'' pipeline as a decision-driven multi-step evolution system. LithoDreamer captures feature changes between adjacent states to model stage-specific physics-informed latent spaces, in which it controls process intervention exploration and drives subsequent state transitions. To achieve interpretable intervention optimization without continuous supervision, we propose a contrastive variational optimization paradigm that contrasts the latent differences between intervention paths with variational evolution constraints, guiding the model to generate evolutions consistent with real lithography physics. Experiments show LithoDreamer achieves state-of-the-art performance in forward evolution and inverse planning.

title: Linkage-Guided Genetic Variation: Overcoming Operator Blindness in Genetic Algorithms
abstract: The core bottleneck of Genetic Algorithms is operator blindness: crossover and mutation locations are chosen at random, routinely breaking valuable building blocks. We introduce the Evolving Locus Linkage Graph (ELLG), which embeds the linkage principle (keep strong segments intact, recombine at weak boundaries) into operator design. At each generation, ELLG updates per-locus linkage weights from observed fitness, producing a task-specific linkage map that tells the algorithm which segments to keep intact and where to cut; as generations proceed, these protected regions and preferred cut sites become increasingly well-defined. A simple monotone transformation converts the learned weights into placement probabilities for crossover and mutation, replacing uniform randomness with targeted, structure-aware operator placement. We integrate ELLG as a plug-in to a standard GA without changing the problem encoding or operator semantics. We benchmark ELLG against a large pool of state-of-the-art evolutionary methods across two domains: classical multi-objective optimization suites and Neural Architecture Search, ELLG achieves higher final solution quality in experiments.

title: Linear-Stability-Guided Two-Stage Surrogate Model for Nonlinear ITG-TEM Turbulence
abstract: We develop a two-stage surrogate model framework to predict the linear and nonlinear properties of ITG-TEM turbulence from GENE gyrokinetic simulations. The first stage uses a hierarchical ensemble of stability and mode classifiers, along with global and mode-specific regressors, to predict the linear growth rate and real frequency. The second stage uses these predictions as linear spectra in a Fourier neural operator (FNO)-based nonlinear surrogate model. The nonlinear model predicts saturated potential and heat flux spectra, together with zonal flow quantities. Two linear drive scalars, the maximum and integral of the linear growth rate over a low-wavenumber range, are also supplied directly to the networks predicting scalar quantities. For the architecture studied here, comparisons with models omitting either or both input paths show that linear information can improve spectral and scalar predictions under extrapolation toward stronger linear drive.

title: Line-tension effect on the equilibrium and stability of a spherical floating particle at a fluid–fluid interface
abstract: A recent matched-asymptotic framework for a spherical particle floating at a fluid–fluid interface reduced the coupled Young equation and vertical force balance to a single nonlinear equation but assumed a constant macroscopic Young angle. We extend the framework to include line tension. A variational derivation places the dimensionless line tension κ=k/(r0σ), the ratio of the line tension k to the product of the sphere radius r0 and the surface tension σ, in the modified Young equation. Because the line-tension energy depends on the filling angle alone and that angle is set by the modified Young equation, the line-tension term drops out of the vertical force balance identically. The coupled system reduces to a single substitution of the constant contact angle by a filling-angle dependent contact angle. Closed-form first-order corrections agree with the numerical solution of the nonlinear asymptotic equilibrium equation with O(κ2) remainders away from the floatability boundary, and the line-tension response of the framework is confirmed independently by a direct numerical solution of the Young–Laplace equation that shares no asymptotic ingredient. The hydrophilic regime is about an order of magnitude more sensitive to κ than the hydrophobic one across the full range of contact angles. The modified Young equation rewrites as a linear regression that recovers k from multi-sphere datasets, and its regression form is shown to be consistent with the original droplet dataset of Klauser and coworkers.

title: Lifelong Learning of Scheduling Rules with Surrogate-assisted Genetic Programming for Dynamic Flexible Job Shop Scheduling
abstract: Genetic programming (GP) has been widely used to learn scheduling rules for dynamic flexible job shop scheduling (DFJSS). However, trained rules tend to only generalise to tasks of similar scales and distributions, and when task characteristics change, learned rules often suffer significant performance degradation. Moreover, fine-tuning pre-trained rules on new tasks often leads to catastrophic forgetting, where prior knowledge is lost. This motivates the need for GP methods that can adapt to new tasks while preserving past knowledge, leading to a lifelong learning paradigm. However, lifelong learning in GP for DFJSS remains largely under-explored. To address this gap, this paper proposes a surrogate-assisted GP method for lifelong learning to handle sequential heterogeneous DFJSS tasks with job or batch arrivals. The framework includes three key components: an adaptive two-stage training strategy to balance plasticity and stability, a task-similarity-based weighting mechanism to regulate knowledge reuse, and an improved surrogate model with distance constraints to enhance estimation accuracy. Experimental results show that the proposed method effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting while maintaining strong adaptability, outperforming several compared methods and demonstrating the potential of lifelong GP in dynamic scheduling environments.

title: Lie-Algebraic Acceleration of Neural Koopman Dynamics
abstract: We present a Lie-algebraic approach to model Koopman dynamics that integrates algebraic structure with computational scalability. The proposed formulation constrains the neural generators to evolve within prescribed Lie subalgebras and constructs finite-time flows through a neural Magnus expansion construction, thereby maintaining consistency with the associated Lie-group composition over each time segment. To address the computational burden inherent in sequential propagation, we exploit the associativity of Lie-group compositions and construct segmentwise propagators via a prefix-scan algorithm, which reduces the depth of temporal composition from linear to logarithmic. Consequently, the framework enables accurate long-horizon prediction while improving computational efficiency, and provides a principled foundation for scalable Koopman operator learning for nonlinear systems.

title: Learning, Solving and Optimizing PDEs with TensorGalerkin: an efficient high-performance Galerkin assembly algorithm
abstract: We present a unified algorithmic framework for the numerical solution, constrained optimization, and physics-informed learning of PDEs with a variational structure. Our framework is based on a Galerkin discretization of the underlying variational forms, and its high efficiency stems from a novel highly-optimized and GPU-compliant TensorGalerkin framework for linear system assembly (stiffness matrices and load vectors). TensorGalerkin operates by tensorizing element-wise operations within a Python-level Map stage and then performs global reduction with a sparse matrix multiplication that performs message passing on the mesh-induced sparsity graph. The Map and Reduce stages are co-designed inside PyTorch's autograd so that the assembly graph contains $O(1)$ nodes regardless of how the number of elements and local DoFs scale. We validate this $O(1)$-graph property by deploying TensorGalerkin downstream as i) a highly-efficient numerical PDEs solver, ii) an end-to-end differentiable framework for PDE-constrained optimization, and iii) a physics-informed operator learning algorithm for PDEs. With multiple benchmarks, including 2D and 3D elliptic, parabolic, and hyperbolic PDEs on unstructured meshes, we demonstrate that the proposed framework provides significant computational efficiency and accuracy gains over a variety of baselines in all the targeted downstream applications.

title: Learning to Unlearn: Machine Unlearning via Learning the Unlearning Behaviors
abstract: Various machine unlearning techniques have been developed in response to privacy legislation requirements. These techniques enable individuals to exercise their legal right to have their data $D_f$ removed from a machine learning model. This process, commonly referred to as machine unlearning, is accomplished via the use of an unlearning function denoted as $U$. Existing methods design an intricate $U$ to unlearn $D_f\subset D$ from a previous model $A(D)$ learned on $D$, so that the unlearned model performs as closely as possible to the retrained model $A(D\setminus D_f)$. However, these methods often take a long time due to the complex structures of $U$. Inspired by Learning to Optimize, in this paper, we introduce the first learning-based model-agnostic approach named Learning-to-UnLearn (or L2UL) based on a distribution perspective, which acquires a simple $U$ via learning. Our experimental results demonstrate that the accuracy achieved by L2UL is comparable to that of retraining, while also exhibiting impressive efficiency.

title: Learning to Think in Physics: Breaking Shortcut Learning in Scientific Diffusion via Representation Alignment
abstract: Physics-informed diffusion models typically enforce PDE constraints only on final outputs, leaving intermediate representations unconstrained and prone to shortcut learning under shifted boundary conditions. We introduce **REPA-P**, a teacher-free, architecture-agnostic framework that aligns intermediate features with physical states using first-principles residuals. REPA-P attaches lightweight $1{\times}1$ projection heads to selected layers, decodes hidden activations into physical quantities, and applies PDE residual losses during training. These heads are discarded at inference, introducing **zero overhead**. Across four PDE tasks, including Darcy flow, topology optimization, electrostatic potential, and turbulent channel flow, REPA-P accelerates convergence by up to $2{\times}$, reduces physics residuals by up to $66.4\%$, and improves out-of-distribution robustness by up to $49.3\%$, with consistent gains on both U-Net and Diffusion Transformer backbones. Ablations show that supervising a small set of intermediate layers captures most benefits and complements output-level physics losses. Code is available at [https://github.com/Hxxxz0/REPA-P](https://github.com/Hxxxz0/REPA-P).

We introduce **REPA-P**, a teacher-free, architecture-agnostic framework that aligns intermediate features with physical states using first-principles residuals. title: Learning the Entropic Relaxation: Stable Coarse-Grid Emulation with Neural Discrete Equilibrium
abstract: The ability to emulate complicated and computationally-expensive physical systems in an efficient and stable manner is a popular motivation for scientific machine learning (SciML). Stable numerical solvers tend to be computationally expensive, as they attempt to resolve small (spatial and temporal) scales that receive and dissipate spectral energy. Learned coarse-grid forecasters remove the dissipative channel, allowing unresolved frequencies to re-emerge as grid-scale noise (aliasing). In this paper, we use the Neural Discrete Equilibrium (NeurDE) method to explore stable emulation at extremely coarse grids, demonstrating physically-principled control over entropy dynamics that reinforces the physical system's dissipative mechanism. Entropically-stabilized NeurDE produces stable long-time rollouts for thousands of forecasting steps on large Reynolds number turbulent flows ($\mathrm{Re}=100{,}000$) with very coarse grids (down to $\mathbb{R}^{16\times16}$). At these very coarse grid scales, entropically-stabilized NeurDE can be more stable than even our stabilized data-generation numerical method.

title: Learning structural response operators across varying geometries and loads with global and local geometry encoding
abstract: Predicting mechanical responses across complex geometries and varying loading conditions is central to simulation-driven engineering, yet capturing the influence of geometric boundaries remains challenging for data-driven models. Here we propose a Load- and Geometry-adaptive Deep Operator Network (LG-DON) that integrates global geometric representations with local, boundary-aware information to predict structural responses. By distinguishing distances to different boundary categories rather than relying on the nearest boundary alone, the framework captures spatially varying geometric influences that conventional distance-based representations may overlook. Across benchmark problems involving diverse non-convex geometries, LG-DON reduces the mean relative L2 error from 12.17% for a modified MIONet baseline to 7.41%. Controlled ablation studies further demonstrate the advantages of category-resolved boundary distances and show that combining global and local geometric representations outperforms either representation alone in 15 of 18 evaluated configurations. These findings highlight the value of integrating complementary geometric information for accurate operator learning across complex structural domains.

title: Learning Where to Learn: Training Data Distribution Optimization for Scientific Machine Learning
abstract: In scientific machine learning, models are routinely deployed with parameter values or boundary conditions far from those used in training. This paper studies the learning-where-to-learn problem of designing a training data distribution that minimizes average prediction error across a family of deployment regimes. A theoretical analysis shows how the training distribution shapes deployment accuracy. This motivates two adaptive algorithms based on bilevel or alternating optimization in the space of probability measures. Discretized implementations using parametric distribution classes or nonparametric particle-based gradient flows deliver optimized training distributions that outperform nonadaptive designs. Once trained, the resulting models exhibit improved sample complexity and robustness to distribution shift. This framework unlocks the potential of principled data acquisition for learning functions and solution operators of partial differential equations.

title: Learning Pseudo-Riemannian Manifolds for Heterophilic Graphs via Graph Signature
abstract: Several widely used families of Graph Neural Networks carry a positive-definite geometric prior. Graph convolution read as heat diffusion needs a positive semi-definite operator, hyperbolic models place features on positive-definite Riemannian manifolds, and dot-product and GAT-style attention scores use positive-definite inner products. On heterophilic graphs, where edges often signify dissimilarity or structural repulsion, that prior is a mismatch: no positive-definite form can assign a negative squared distance to a direction the labels separate. To measure the mismatch, we introduce the Graph Signature Index ($s_{\mathcal{G}}$), the inertia of a class-compatibility matrix built from label topology alone, and we prove that no value of the edge or node homophily index in $(0,1)$ rules out a negative eigenvalue. We then propose the Pseudo-Riemannian Attention Network (PRAT), whose attention logit is a signed squared pseudo-distance under a learnable diagonal metric initialized from $s_{\mathcal{G}}$. The design is diagnose-then-learn: the signature supplies a sign structure that unconstrained training keeps outside near-zero directions, and the projection learns the rest of the metric around it. Across fifteen node-classification benchmarks PRAT outperforms or matches the strongest heterophily-adapted models. A controlled ablation ties that performance to the sign structure itself: with architecture and protocol fixed, forbidding the metric to be indefinite costs accuracy on the graphs $s_{\mathcal{G}}$ marks as indefinite and leaves the others unchanged.

title: Learning Nonlocal Interactions in Large-Scale Heterogeneous Metamaterials through Scientific Machine Learning
abstract: In multiscale systems, nonlocal interactions among spatially distributed constituents can unlock collective, potentially emergent behavior irreducible to individual constituent responses. Beyond characterization, nonlocality in multiscale systems is increasingly viewed as a design element across fracture mechanics, wave physics, and disordered systems. Existing nonlocality theories provide rigorous descriptions and mechanistic insight, but often require prescribed analytic forms, range, symmetries, or periodicity. Machine learning offers a data-driven route to learn interactions, yet principled approaches that tie the network design to physical theory remain nascent. Here we present domain-decomposition attention neural operator (DANO), which learns configuration-dependent interactions in heterogeneous systems governed by linear field equations from field data alone. Through a case study in large-scale optical metasurfaces, we demonstrate DANO's full-field prediction under geometric heterogeneity and across drive conditions, small-to-large domain transfer, and multifunctional inverse design, with learned interactions validated through physics-based interrogation. As an AI-for-Science tool, it supports interaction discovery and scalable, customizable design of nonlocal multiscale systems, including virtual-reality optics.

title: Learning Kolmogorov Backward Operators for Spectral Analysis and Forecasting: A Data-Driven Variational Galerkin Framework
abstract: For a time-homogeneous Markov process, the fixed-lag solution operator \( (T_τf)(x)=\mathbb E[f(X_{t+τ})\mid X_t=x] \) of the Kolmogorov backward equation evolves observables linearly and deterministically, even when the dynamics are stochastic. We approximate this operator using a two-stage method where we first approximate this operator directly from data, without knowledge of the governing equation (e.g., Fourier Neural Operator), and then compress the Galerkin projection onto a finite-dimensional observable space that is fixed in advance or selected variationally. The error analysis traces the learning error of the estimator, the sampling error of the Galerkin inner products, and the invariance and reconstruction properties of the observable space to the computed spectra and forecasts. The sampling error enters only through a multiplicative factor. Near an isolated spectral cluster, the invariance defect of a subspace controls its distance from the target invariant subspace. The forecast error is controlled by the one-step error of the reduced model and the projection error of the observable; when the measure is invariant and the reduced model preserves constants and is stable on mean-zero observables, the bound is uniform in the horizon. For deterministic dynamics, a learning rate for Fourier neural operators (FNOs) gives one explicit bound for the learning error. Numerical experiments illustrate spectral approximation and forecasting, including long-rollout stability and a comparison with extended dynamic mode decomposition (EDMD) when fewer transition pairs than basis functions are observed.

title: Learning Implicit Solves for Dynamic Simulations
abstract: High-fidelity simulation of dynamical systems is central to scientific discovery and engineering design, yet remains computationally demanding. Here we introduce the Implicit Neural Operator Solver (INOS), which learns the implicit solve and encodes a time integrator. INOS pretrains a neural operator from static equilibrium solutions and reuses it within Newmark-$β$ integration. At each time increment, the integrator forms an effective equilibrium problem, the pretrained neural operator infers the next-step solution field, and the Newmark relations advance the dynamic state. Numerical examples in linear and nonlinear elastodynamics demonstrate accurate full-field predictions without dynamic trajectory supervision. Comparative results show that INOS, evaluated zero-shot, achieves higher predictive accuracy than neural solver baselines trained on dynamic simulations. In addition, INOS delivers over 4,600$\times$ speedup in nonlinear simulations over sequential classical finite-element solvers. INOS natively accommodates changes in dynamic conditions and enables reuse of the pretrained operator across spatial and temporal discretizations. Further evaluation demonstrates a stable million-step rollout. These findings establish INOS as a reusable neural implicit solver for accurate, efficient, and robust dynamic modeling.

title: Learning Data-Efficient and Generalizable Neural Operators via Fundamental Physics Knowledge
abstract: Recent advances in scientific machine learning (SciML) have enabled neural operators (NOs) to serve as powerful surrogates for modeling the dynamic evolution of physical systems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs). While existing approaches focus primarily on learning simulations from the target PDE, they often overlook more fundamental physical principles underlying these equations. Inspired by how numerical solvers are compatible with simulations of different settings of PDEs, we propose a multiphysics training framework that jointly learns from both the original PDEs and their simplified basic forms. Our framework enhances data efficiency, reduces predictive errors, and improves out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, particularly in scenarios involving shifts of physical parameters and synthetic-to-real transfer. Our method is architecture-agnostic and demonstrates consistent improvements in normalized root mean square error (nRMSE) across a wide range of 1D/2D/3D PDE problems. Through extensive experiments, we show that explicit incorporation of fundamental physics knowledge significantly strengthens the generalization ability of neural operators. We will release models and codes at https://sites.google.com/view/sciml-fundemental-pde.

title: Learned Warm Starts for Steady Transonic RANS Simulations of Wing and Aircraft Configurations
abstract: Neural surrogates can accelerate many-query aerodynamic analyses, but their standalone predictions may be insufficiently accurate or robust to support reliable design evaluations. We develop a learned warm-start formulation that predicts mean-flow and turbulence fields directly on native CFD meshes for subsequent correction by the RANS solver. A common architecture and objective structure are used across subcritical and transonic flows, including challenging conditions with shock-induced separation. A condition-modulated Transolver combines Fourier and wall features with target-gated regularization, a Sobolev-type loss, adaptive loss weighting and sampled training. Prediction requires no preliminary flow solution, and training requires no solver-residual evaluation. Extensive 3D CFD evaluations on SuperWing, the NASA Common Research Model (CRM) and DLR-F6 assess geometric and operating-condition generalization, including interpolation, extrapolation and cross-mesh deployment, using Spalart-Allmaras and $k$-$ω$ SST closures on million-cell meshes. Unseen nominal cases achieve geometric-mean iteration speed-ups of approximately $2$-$4\times$ under a common convergence criterion based on cold-run aerodynamic coefficients. On CRM, learned initialization provides greater aggregate acceleration than nearest-condition restarts using the same solution library. Resolution invariance enables direct deployment of coarse-mesh models on finer meshes without retraining, solution interpolation or target-condition coarse solves. Including data generation and training, estimated campaign speed-ups reach $2.1$-$2.3\times$. No warm run diverges; fewer than $2\%$ fail to satisfy the cold-reference convergence criterion. These results support learned initialization for repeated aerodynamic analyses, while highlighting initialization sensitivity near separation as a remaining limitation.

title: Learned Surrogates of Three-Dimensional Magnetohydrodynamic Turbulence
abstract: Three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence, the flow of astrophysical and fusion plasmas, is costly to simulate. We present, to our knowledge, the first learned surrogates of three-dimensional resistive MHD turbulence, and compare three standard backbones in that role: a convolutional UNet, a shifted-window transformer and a Fourier neural operator. They are trained as autoregressive emulators of decaying MHD turbulence at a resolution of $128^3$ and Reynolds numbers of 1000, 3000 and 6000, on 500 simulations per Reynolds number, each with one two-stage procedure, single steps and then short rollouts, and stopped by one rule. Over a window of about one large-eddy turnover time, the UNet and the transformer reach relative velocity errors of 0.018 to 0.053 and keep the current sheets, the enstrophy, the current density and the energy spectra of the simulation; which of the two is the more accurate depends on the Reynolds number, the UNet leading at 3000 and 6000 and the transformer at 1000. Applied with the same backbones and training procedure to two public benchmarks, the models reach the lowest error reported to date on the isotropic turbulence set of FactFormer, 39% below the best published model. On the compressible MHD set of The Well, their rollout errors are a third to a half below those of the best of The Well's baselines. They also match a 1.3 B-parameter pretrained foundation model in its rollout windows, with 20-62 times fewer parameters. The code, the configuration of every model, the evaluation scripts and the data generator with the seed of every simulation will be released upon publication.

title: Leakage-free evaluation of residual graph convolutional networks for network intrusion detection
abstract: Graph neural networks are increasingly proposed for network intrusion detection, yet many reported results come from protocols in which test flows shape the graph used for training, duplicated flows sit on both sides of the split, or a single split is reported. This study measures what a residual graph convolutional network gains over simpler models once these sources of optimism are removed. CICIDS2017 and NF-UNSW-NB15-v2 were cleaned with label-aware removal of exact duplicates, removing 69% of NF-UNSW-NB15-v2 flows. Flows were linked in a nearest-neighbour graph built from training flows only, and validation and test flows were attached to their nearest training flows at prediction time. A two-layer residual network was compared with eight models under the same settings, including a nearest-neighbour vote over the same graph, gradient-boosted trees and a random forest, over three seeds that each draw a new split, with ablations, leave-one-family-out and feature-noise tests. On CICIDS2017 the residual network reached a binary F1 of 98.11% (SD 0.18) and on NF-UNSW-NB15-v2 90.57% (0.38), indistinguishable from a multilayer perceptron without the graph and from other graph networks. Tree ensembles were 1.48 to 1.57 F1 points higher on CICIDS2017 and led on the area under the precision-recall curve on both datasets; their CICIDS2017 multiclass macro-F1 reached 93.08% against 64.51%, a gap mainly from benign flows the residual network assigned to small attack classes. No ablation, including transductive graph construction, changed F1 beyond seed variation. Under Gaussian feature noise (SD 0.5), the residual network kept an F1 of 96.16%, while XGBoost fell to 0.67%. Under a leakage-controlled protocol, message passing over flow graphs adds no measurable accuracy over a perceptron, and tree ensembles remain stronger on both; the advantage of graph models lies in robustness to feature noise.

title: Latent Space Learning for PDE Systems with Complex Boundary Conditions
abstract: Latent space Reduced Order Models (ROMs) in Scientific Machine Learning (SciML) can enhance and accelerate Partial Differential Equation (PDE) simulations. However, they often struggle with complex boundary conditions (BCs) such as time-varying, nonlinear, or state-dependent ones. Current methods for handling BCs in latent space have limitations due to representation mismatch and projection difficulty, impacting predictive accuracy and physical consistency. To address this, we introduce BAROM (Boundary-Aware Attention ROM). BAROM integrates: (1) explicit, RBM-inspired boundary treatment using a modified ansatz and a learnable lifting network for complex BCs; and (2) a non-intrusive, attention-based mechanism, inspired by Galerkin Neural Operators, to learn internal field dynamics within a POD-initialized latent space. Evaluations show BAROM achieves superior accuracy and robustness on benchmark PDEs with diverse complex BCs compared to established SciML approaches.

title: Latent PDE Mapping for Shape-Generalizable Physics-Informed Neural Networks
abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have shown strong potential for learning physically consistent representations from sparse data, but often struggle to generalize to geometries with varying shapes. To address this challenge, we introduce $\textit{latent PDE mapping}$, a technique for mapping geometry-specific partial differential equations (PDEs) to a shared latent PDE representation using the deformation gradient. We embed latent PDE mapping into the PINN framework (LPM-PINN), enabling PINNs to capture geometric variability while preserving the governing physics. This integration facilitates accurate predictions of nonlinear, time-dependent systems even in geometries well beyond the training distribution. We demonstrate LPM-PINN on a challenging nonlinear time-dependent PDE with sharp gradients, the Aliev–Panfilov model of cardiac electrophysiology, in both 2D and 3D. Our results show that LPM-PINN generalizes robustly across diverse geometries, including shapes with drastically changing boundaries that lie outside the training distribution. These findings establish latent PDE mapping as a promising approach for boosting the geometric generalizability of physics-informed neural networks.

title: Laser- and shock-induced droplet dynamics: A machine learning benchmark for complex multiphase flows
abstract: Compressible multiphase flow is central to numerous engineering applications, characterized by complex wave dynamics and challenging shock-interface interactions. Despite their importance, they remain significantly missing from existing benchmarks in the Scientific Machine Learning (SciML) community, limiting progress on generalization to impactful real-world scenarios. To address this issue, we introduce two exemplary datasets from this class, Laser-Induced Droplet Explosion (LIDE) and Shock-Induced Droplet Aero-breakup (SIDA), providing researchers with valuable references to establish reliable baselines and push boundaries of SciML. Due to the high computational cost of simulating these processes with full fidelity, we explore data-driven surrogate models designed to efficiently approximate the underlying physics at reduced cost. We benchmark these datasets on diverse architectures trained autoregressively and compared across varying parameter counts. A comprehensive set of ablations is carried out to analyze the performance of the models. We identify key scenarios, such as incorporating temporal sequence information and conditioning, that enable the models to accurately capture the rich and nonlinear physics embedded in the datasets. Code and datasets will be made publically available upon acceptance.

title: Large-scale identification of the regulatory potential of SNPs in human neural stem cells
abstract: Abstract GWAS have identified thousands of SNPs associated with different human phenotypes. Most SNPs are located in non-coding regions of the genome, where a small subset of causal SNPs is thought to contribute to risk by regulating transcription. However, identification of such causal variants remains challenging due to linkage disequilibrium, where blocks of SNPs are inherited together. Here, we perform a massively parallel reporter assay called SuRE in human neural stem cells to assess the transcriptional regulatory potential of 7.1 million SNPs. We identify 7,002 SNPs with regulatory potential (emVars) among the 484,057 SNPs with sufficiently high expression. These emVars are enriched in enhancers and often coincide with binding sites for transcription factors, such as ZBTB33, YY1, and ETS factors. We overlap SuRE data with eQTL data to pinpoint likely gene-regulatory variants. Additionally, combining SuRE data with GWAS for seven neuropsychiatric phenotypes identifies 187 emVars in risk loci containing 183,186 SNPs assessed by SuRE. In conclusion, our SuRE dataset provides a rich source to prioritize genetic variants that may be relevant for complex human phenotypes.

title: Large-Scale Bayesian Optimisation Using Uncertainty-Calibrated Product-of-Experts Gaussian Process Models with Trust Regions
abstract: The use of collections of independent local Gaussian processes (GP-ind) combined with trust regions is a widely adopted approach for large-scale and high-dimensional Bayesian optimisation (BO). However, this approach suffers from several limitations, including discontinuities at the boundaries of disjoint regions, an inability to capture long-range spatial correlations, potential information loss, and abrupt increases in computational overhead. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a novel BO algorithm, termed BO-pro-c-tr. The proposed method employs a product-of-experts Gaussian process model with uncertainty calibration (GP-pro-c) as its surrogate model and incorporates a one-to-many association strategy for integrating GP-pro-c with trust regions. Empirical results suggest that, when combined with the GP-LCB acquisition function, BO-pro-c-tr achieves an average reduction of 2.6% in simple regret and 34.9% in computational overhead relative to BO algorithms based on independent local GP models coupled with trust regions.

title: Lang-PINN: From Language to Physics-Informed Neural Networks via a Multi-Agent Framework
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a powerful approach for solving partial differential equations (PDEs), but constructing a usable PINN remains labor-intensive and error-prone. Scientists must interpret problems as PDE formulations, design architectures and loss functions, and implement stable training pipelines. Existing large language model (LLM) approaches address isolated steps such as code generation or architecture suggestion, but typically assume a formal PDE is already specified and therefore lack an end-to-end perspective. We present **Lang-PINN**, an LLM-driven multi-agent system that builds trainable PINNs directly from natural language task descriptions. **Lang-PINN** coordinates four complementary agents: a \emph{PDE Agent} that parses task descriptions into symbolic PDEs, a \emph{PINN Agent} that selects architectures, a \emph{Code Agent} that generates modular implementations, and a \emph{Feedback Agent} that executes and diagnoses errors for iterative refinement. This design transforms informal task statements into executable and verifiable PINN code. Experiments show that **Lang-PINN** achieves substantially lower errors and greater robustness than competitive baselines: mean squared error (MSE) is reduced by up to 3–5 orders of magnitude, end-to-end execution success improves by more than 50\%, and reduces time overhead by up to 74\%.

title: LOCA: Logical Chain Augmentation for Scientific Corpus Cleaning
abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in general domains, their reliability often falls short in scientific problem-solving. The advancement of scientific AI depends on large-scale, high-quality corpora. However, existing scientific question-answering (QA) datasets suffer from high error rates, frequently resulting from logical leaps and implicit reasoning within the answers. To address this issue, we introduce LOCA (Logical Chain Augmentation), a novel framework for automatically cleaning scientific corpora, implemented through an augment-and-review loop. At its core, LOCA enhances raw answers by completing missing logical steps and explicitly separating the underlying scientific principle from its subsequent derivation. By applying LOCA to challenging scientific corpora, we demonstrate that it can automatically filter noisy datasets, typically reducing the error rate from as high as 20\% to below 2\%. LOCA provides a scalable and effective methodology for creating high-quality scientific corpora, paving the way for more reliable training and evaluation of scientific AI.

title: LM6-CastBench: A Geometry-Aware Simulation Dataset for Transient Thermal Prediction in LM6 Sand Casting
abstract: Transient thermal fields during solidification connect casting process conditions and cooling behaviour to the formation of defect-prone regions in aluminum cast ings. Repeatedly solving this thermal problem across geometries and process conditions is computationally expensive, motivating data-driven surrogate models. However, existing machine-learning studies on casting thermal behaviour rely on study-specific simulation databases that do not support reproducible geometry-level benchmarking. We introduce LM6-CastBench, an open simulation dataset for geometry-aware learning of transient thermal fields in LM6 aluminum sand casting, combining three geometry families, ten variants per family, five pouring tempera tures, and three mould temperatures (450 geometry-process cases in total). Each case retains CAD geometry, unstructured mesh connectivity, spatial descriptors, process metadata, and time-resolved nodal temperatures. We benchmark a point wise MLP against a spatially structured U-Net under geometry-level data splits; the U-Net reduces temperature-field errors by a large margin, with the biggest gains on geometries with localized features and abrupt section changes. LM6-CastBench gives researchers a reproducible dataset and benchmark for geometry-aware surro gate modelling of casting thermal behaviour.

title: LFNO: Bridging Laplace and Fourier for Effective Operator Learning
abstract: We introduce Laplace–Fourier Neural Operator (LFNO), a novel operator learning model that bridges the strengths of Laplace Neural Operators (LNO) and Fourier Neural Operators (FNO). By combining the transient response of LNO with the steady-state response of FNO through the Fourier integral operator, our model enables capturing transient behavior more effectively than both LNO and FNO while remaining comparable on linear and nonlinear PDEs. We demonstrate LFNO's effectiveness on solving three ODEs (Duffing, Lorenz, Pendulum) and five PDEs (Euler-Bernoulli beam, diffusion, reaction-diffusion, Brusselator, Gray-Scott) in comparison to FNO and LNO. These results highlight LFNO’s ability to unify transient and steady-state modeling, delivering superior accuracy and stability across various dynamical systems.

title: LENS: Reliability-Aware Stock Prediction via LLM-Extracted Priors and News-Driven Semantic Graphs
abstract: Predicting stock returns requires modeling persistent company relations and time-varying market signals. Graph Neural Network (GNN) approaches combine static priors with dynamic relational graphs, but treat every extracted edge as a trustworthy binary fact, ignoring heterogeneous reliability across relational sources. We propose LENS (LLM-Extracted priors and News-driven Semantics), a static--dynamic graph framework for stock return prediction and ranking that models relational reliability as a first-class signal across the pipeline. On the static side, we extract a multi-relational company graph from a Large Language Model and aggregate it over multiple runs with confidence weighting to downweight low-consistency edges. On the dynamic side, we build a news-driven semantic graph with exponential-decay temporal aggregation to capture changing market context under uneven coverage. A context-dependent gated fusion module rebalances the two graphs at the per-stock, per-day level. On S&P 500, LENS improves AR@5 by 16.4% and SR@5 by 22.6% over the strongest baseline, and on NASDAQ 100 it achieves comparable improvements (15.5% and 20.9% respectively). Ablations isolate each component's contribution, and a human-validation study of sampled relations supports that the aggregation is grounded, providing evidence that reliability-aware LLM relations and news-based semantic graphs carry complementary information for graph-based financial prediction.

Graph Neural Network (GNN) approaches combine static priors with dynamic relational graphs, but treat every extracted edge as a trustworthy binary fact, ignoring heterogeneous reliability across relational sources. We propose LENS (LLM-Extracted priors and News-driven Semantics), a static--dynamic graph framework…

title: Kernel-based Interpolatory Methods for Context Compression of Attention Mechanisms
abstract: The bottleneck of attention mechanisms, which are the fundamental building block of modern language models, is their quadratic complexity in terms of context size. There has thus been an increasing interest in the compression of the context, also called KV-cache compression. In this article, we consider the problem of compressing the context of attention mechanisms by first formulating it in the Hilbert space associated with its kernel. In this formalism, attention can be represented as the ratio of two linear maps whose interpolant is also the ratio of interpolants, this allows us to consider the interpolation of the linear maps directly. We thus introduce two novel KV-cache compression methods which we call GAIM and Q-DAIM, based on the Generalized Empirical Interpolation Method (GEIM) and the Q-Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method (Q-DEIM), respectively. As the cost of these methods is quadratic in terms of context length, we propose surrogate models based on the Taylor series, the Performer and the Random Fourier Features method which allow the compression to be done in linear time. Finally, we extend this result to the streaming attention setting, providing new methods which allow one to penalize the selection of interpolation nodes based on the previously interpolated context and to update the previous interpolation based on new information. We then provide numerical results on the convergence of the residuals and the output error in future queries and preliminary results on the LongBench-E benchmark showing performance comparable to the state-of-the-art methods. These experiments suggest that the range revealed by our Q-DAIM method could help identify where information is concentrated in the KV cache, thus enabling an efficient compression.

title: KANO: Kolmogorov-Arnold Neural Operator
abstract: We introduce Kolmogorov–Arnold Neural Operator (KANO), a dual‑domain neural operator jointly parameterized by both spectral and spatial bases with intrinsic symbolic interpretability. We theoretically demonstrate that KANO overcomes the pure-spectral bottleneck of Fourier Neural Operator (FNO): KANO remains expressive over a generic position-dependent dynamics for any physical input, whereas FNO stays practical only to spectrally sparse operators and strictly imposes fast-decaying input Fourier tail. We verify our claims empirically on position-dependent differential operators, for which KANO robustly generalizes but FNO fails to. In the quantum Hamiltonian learning benchmark, KANO reconstructs ground‑truth Hamiltonians in closed-form symbolic representations accurate to the fourth decimal place in coefficients and attains $\approx6\times10^{-6}$ state infidelity from projective measurement data, substantially outperforming that of the FNO trained with ideal full wave function data, $\approx1.5\times10^{-2}$, by orders of magnitude.

title: JanusPipe: Efficient Pipeline Parallel Training for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
abstract: Discovering atom-level phenomena requires molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with ab initio accuracy. Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) enable stable, high-accuracy MD simulations, and their models exhibit scaling-law trends similar to large language models. However, the lack of scalable and efficient distributed training systems for conservative MLIPs makes them difficult to scale. This is because conservative MLIPs inherently follow a double-backward execution pattern, which involves computing gradients during the forward pass. This pattern creates a mismatch with existing distributed training systems, especially for pipeline parallelism. Therefore, we present JanusPipe, an efficient 3D-parallel (PP/DP/GP) training system tailored for conservative MLIPs. It integrates SymFold to enable memory-efficient pipeline parallelism for conservative MLIPs, and WaveK to reduce pipeline bubbles by balancing the four-phase compute time. Experimental results on 32 GPUs show that JanusPipe improves throughput by $1.51\times$ and $1.45\times$ on average over 1F1B and Hanayo, respectively.

title: Iterative Training of Physics-Informed Neural Networks with Fourier-enhanced Features
abstract: Spectral bias, the tendency of neural networks to learn low-frequency features first, is a well-known issue with many training algorithms for physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). To overcome this issue, we propose IFeF-PINN, an algorithm for iterative training of PINNs with Fourier-enhanced features. The key idea is to enrich the latent space using high-frequency components through Random Fourier Features. This creates a two-stage training problem: (i) estimate a basis in the feature space, and (ii) perform regression to determine the coefficients of the enhanced basis functions. For an underlying linear model, it is shown that the latter problem is convex, and we prove that the iterative training scheme converges. Furthermore, we empirically establish that Random Fourier Features enhance the expressive capacity of the network, enabling accurate approximation of high-frequency PDEs. Through extensive numerical evaluation on classical benchmark problems, the superior performance of our method over state-of-the-art algorithms is shown, and the improved approximation across the frequency domain is illustrated.

title: Iterative Refinement Neural Operators are Learned Fixed-Point Solvers: A Principled Approach to Spectral Bias Mitigation
abstract: Neural operators serve as fast, data-driven surrogates for scientific modeling but typically rely on a monolithic, single-pass inference procedure that struggles to resolve high-frequency details, a limitation known as spectral bias. We introduce the Iterative Refinement Neural Operator (IRNO), which augments pre-trained operators with a learned refinement module iteratively applied via fixed-point iteration. IRNO decomposes the prediction into a coarse initialization followed by successive residual corrections, paralleling classical numerical solvers. Under mild assumptions, we establish contraction of the induced operator, ensuring convergence to a unique fixed point. To explicitly target high-frequency errors, we propose a progressive spectral loss that adaptively increases penalty on high-frequency components over refinement steps during training. Across physical systems, IRNO consistently lowers error, with up to 56.05\% improvement on turbulent flow. On Active Matter, spectral analysis reveals that, relative to base operator, the normalized error ratios decrease to 27.72–36.10\% in low-, 5.07–6.68\% in mid-, and 1.48–2.04\% in high-frequencies, remaining stable beyond the trained iteration count.

title: Interpretable structural temperature scaling for calibrating graph neural networks and point-cloud segmentation
abstract: Graph-aware calibrators make graph neural networks (GNNs) more trustworthy by predicting a temperature for each node, usually with auxiliary networks whose decisions are hard to inspect. We propose Interpretable Structural Temperature Scaling (ISTS), a twelve-parameter linear model that sets each node's temperature from named descriptors of its confidence, neighbourhood and closeness to labelled nodes, so every temperature traces back to descriptor contributions. ISTS preserves predictions, and cross-validated regularisation lets the calibration data decide how far the model departs from temperature scaling (TS). Its explanations are faithful at the level of node groups: on test nodes, ISTS softens groups that a global temperature leaves over-confident and sharpens under-confident ones (Spearman correlation 0.67 over 246 groups). On seven graphs with two backbones and eleven baselines, ISTS has the best average rank in negative log-likelihood (NLL) and Brier score and lowers NLL relative to TS by 1.8%, more than twice the gain of an identically fitted entropy-based temperature. It ranked first again on four held-out graphs under a protocol fixed in advance. From about 100 calibration nodes on, ISTS is a cheap and inspectable choice, and on point-cloud segmentation it significantly improves NLL, Brier score and the ranking of points for rejection.

title: Interpretability and Generalization Bounds for Learning Spatial Physics
abstract: While there are many applications of machine learning (ML) to scientific problems that \emph{look} promising, the eye test can be misleading compared to the quantitative values. Using numerical analysis techniques, we rigorously quantify the accuracy, convergence rates, and generalization bounds of certain ML models applied to linear differential equations (DEs) for parameter discovery or solution finding. Beyond the quantity and discretization of data, we identify that the {function space} of the data is critical to the generalization of the model which can lead to divergence. Similar lack of generalization is empirically demonstrated for commonly used models. Surprisingly, we find that different classes of models can exhibit opposing generalization behaviors. Based on our theoretical analysis, we also introduce a new mechanistic interpretability lens on scientific models whereby Green's function representations can be extracted from the weights of black-box models. Our results inform a new cross-validation technique for measuring generalization in physical systems, and can be useful as a benchmark of future methods.

title: Interactive World Simulation with Cosmos for Physical AI
abstract: We present a shared framework that adapts Cosmos world foundation models for real-time interactive world simulation in Physical AI. By streaming visual observations in response to actions and scene controls, the framework enables users and embodied agents to interact with evolving virtual environments. It supports both predicting the visual consequences of actions and generating observations from physical state maintained by an external simulator. We demonstrate this approach across camera navigation and robot manipulation, controllable video transfer, and multi-view autonomous vehicle (AV) simulation. These examples provide a shared foundation for developing interactive virtual environments for Physical AI training and evaluation. Our code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/nvidia/cosmos and https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/cosmos3-examples. The project website is available at https://research.nvidia.com/labs/cosmos-lab/cosmos-simulation.

title: InteractScience: Programmatic and Visually-Grounded Evaluation of Interactive Scientific Demonstration Code Generation
abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) hold promise for automating science and education, generating interactive scientific demonstrations demands a complex synthesis of deep domain knowledge and precise reactive coding. Current benchmarks fail to capture this synergy, largely bifurcating into static code generation or text-only reasoning. To address this, we introduce \textsc{InteractScience}, the first benchmark dedicated to evaluating the holistic creation of interactive scientific applications. We propose a novel hybrid framework that integrates programmatic functional testing for logic verification with visually-grounded qualitative assessment for rendering fidelity. Our evaluation of 30 leading models across five disciplines reveals critical gaps in grounding scientific reasoning within interactive interfaces. By standardizing this combined capability, \textsc{InteractScience} establishes a crucial foundation for reliable AI-driven tools in science and education.

title: Inter-cavity flame dynamics for ignition and flameholding in a dual-cavity scramjet
abstract: To investigate the effects of ignition position on flame propagation and combustion characteristics in a dual-cavity scramjet combustor, comparative experiments were conducted under upstream cavity ignition (UCI) and downstream cavity ignition (DCI) conditions in a direct-connect supersonic combustor facility at an inflow Mach number of 2.52. Synchronized schlieren and CH* chemiluminescence imaging systems were employed to visualize flow and flame dynamics during ignition and flameholding processes. For both ignition positions in the present study, the flame initially propagates downstream, then migrates upstream, and finally stabilizes above the upstream cavity. During inter-cavity propagation, the flame leading edge anchors in the near-wall low-velocity zone, and the flame propagation path within the unignited cavity follows the local recirculation direction. Combustion-induced backpressure shifts the shock train upstream; the resulting shock–flame interaction enhances flame propagation toward the unignited cavity and intensifies combustion during the first inter-cavity propagation in the DCI case, whereas this phenomenon is not observed in the UCI case. During flameholding, both cases exhibit cyclic oscillations with temporary flame weakening near the downstream cavity. Under UCI, the oscillation frequency progressively increases until premature flameout occurs, while under DCI, the frequency remains lower without acceleration; both cavities provide stronger flame stabilization, and the flame leading edge oscillates over a smaller range.

title: Integrating Machine Learning and Uncertainty Quantification for Real-Time Decision-Making in Digital Twins: A System-Centric Review and Perspective
abstract: Digital Twins are evolving from passive virtual representations into closed-loop systems that continuously synchronize with physical assets and drive real-time decisions. Yet predictive modeling, machine learning (ML), uncertainty quantification (UQ), and decision-making have been studied as separate capabilities, leaving limited understanding of their integration and maintenance during online operation. This narrative review, scoped by the functional requirements of real-time decision-making rather than by Digital Twin terminology alone, examines how such decisions are generated and sustained in engineering Digital Twins. We first examine foundational decision-making architectures and representative engineering applications, followed by methods that address their limitations across the decision loop. We identify optimization-based, policy-based, and knowledge-based approaches as the major pathways from virtual representation to action. Across them, ML plays three roles in decision-making: enabling efficient surrogate modeling, transforming heterogeneous physical feedback into decision-relevant information, and accelerating or directly generating decisions. UQ supports uncertainty-aware decisions and model adaptation, while continual validation, drift detection, and adaptation help maintain reliable operation as the physical system evolves. Together, these findings underscore the need for a shift from a model-centric to a system-centric perspective on Digital Twins, where its performance depends on the interactions with sensing, state estimation, computation, decision-making, and adaptation rather than on their standalone performance. Therefore, future research should shift from isolated algorithm development toward system-level co-design, scalable decision-making, and approaches to design, and data-efficient continual adaptation and validation for AI-enabled autonomous systems.

title: Inherent Failure Modes of Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Buoyancy-Driven Flow: Role of Non-Dimensionalization in Network Training
abstract: We investigate the influence of non-dimensionalization on the trainability and accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for buoyancy-driven flows. Using a differentially heated square cavity at $\mathrm{Pr}=0.71$ and $\mathrm{Ra}=10^3$--$10^5$, we compare thermal-diffusive and free-fall velocity scalings under identical training conditions. The free-fall scaling, with a unit buoyancy coefficient, achieves errors below 1.1\% in the mean Nusselt number for $\mathrm{Ra}\le10^4$, whereas the diffusive scaling, with a buoyancy coefficient of $\mathrm{Ra}\,\mathrm{Pr}$, produces errors of 157--650\% and diverges at $\mathrm{Ra}=10^5$. We identify a coefficient-induced gradient imbalance, with the dominant buoyancy-related contribution to the loss gradient scaling as $(\mathrm{Ra}\,\mathrm{Pr})^2$, and confirm it through direct gradient measurements. Neither sparse-data supervision nor adaptive loss weighting resolves the training difficulties under the tested conditions. For unsteady convection, the free-fall PINN accurately predicts long-time heat transfer but fails to capture the transient Nusselt-number overshoot. These findings establish non-dimensionalization as an important design consideration for improving PINN trainability in buoyancy-driven flows.

title: Influence of back-blade structure on axial force and flow characteristics of a centrifugal pump
abstract: Axial force critically affects the operational stability, bearing load and service life of centrifugal pumps, and back blades on the rear shroud are a widely adopted effective measure for axial-force mitigation. This work systematically explores the influences of curved back-blade configurations on pump hydraulic performance, axial-force variation, and internal flow structures via experiments coupled with steady and unsteady numerical simulations. One prototype impeller with balance holes and four curved back-blade impellers are tested under five flow conditions from 0.25Qd to 1.25Qd. The numerical method is validated against experimental data, with maximum relative errors of 3.25% for pump head and 8.51% for axial force. Eight newly designed impellers with varied back-blade counts and phase offsets are further simulated to analyze axial-force-flow characteristics. Curved back blades raise pump head but slightly reduce hydraulic efficiency. Notably, axial force presents a non-monotonic hump-shaped variation with flow rate, peaking at 0.75Qd for fully aligned back-blade impellers. The phase offset between main and back blades is identified as the dominant factor governing the hump. Aligned back blades intensify rotor–stator interaction, drive the primary vortex to precess toward the front-shroud clearance, amplify leakage, and induce a sharp front-shroud pressure drop, while phase-offset back blades suppress such interaction and eliminate the hump. These findings provide physical insight and practical guidance for back-blade optimization in centrifugal pump axial-force control.

title: Inertial gravity currents released from a lock in frames under horizontal oscillations: Analytical model
abstract: We consider the flow of a gravity current released from a lock inside a tank which performs horizontal oscillations (equivalent to internal pressure-gradient pulses), in the buoyancy–inertia (high-Reynolds-number) regime. We develop a shallow-water model which provides clear-cut insights and simple predictions of the propagation, height and velocity fields as a function of time, for a wide range of parameters. Comparisons with the simulations of Bingol et al. (2025 J. Fluid. Mech. , vol. 1002, A14) support the approximate analysis. Moreover, we point out a new effect, called pulse-buoyancy, which was not covered by these simulation. The clear-cut predictions of the model are amenable to straightforward experimental verification, and suggest further numerical work for an as yet unexplored parameter range.

title: Imposing Boundary Conditions on Neural Operators via Learned Function Extensions
abstract: Neural operators have emerged as powerful surrogates for the solution of partial differential equations (PDEs), yet their ability to handle general, highly variable boundary conditions (BCs) remains limited. Existing approaches often fail when the solution operator exhibits strong sensitivity to boundary forcings. We propose a general framework for conditioning neural operators on complex non-homogeneous BCs through function extensions. Our key idea is to map boundary data to latent pseudo-extensions defined over the entire spatial domain, enabling any standard operator learning architecture to consume boundary information. The resulting operator, coupled with an arbitrary domain-to-domain neural operator, can learn rich dependencies on complex BCs and input domain functions at the same time. To benchmark this setting, we construct 18 challenging datasets spanning Poisson, linear elasticity, and hyperelasticity problems, with highly variable, mixed-type, component-wise, and multi-segment BCs on diverse geometries. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, outperforming baselines by large margins, while requiring no hyperparameter tuning across datasets. Overall, our results demonstrate that learning boundary-to-domain extensions is an effective and practical strategy for imposing complex BCs in existing neural operator frameworks, enabling accurate and robust scientific machine learning models for a broader range of PDE-governed problems.

title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints
abstract: The shear piezoelectric coefficient $e_{15}$ governs the shear-mode electromechanical coupling in piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (PMUTs) and surface acoustic wave (SAW) devices, but measuring it typically requires destructive resonance testing on dedicated specimens. On simulated data, $e_{15}$ can instead be recovered non-destructively from sparse, noisy subsurface wavefield observations using a constrained physics-informed neural network (PINN). By building exact spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers directly into the network output, the clamped, grounded boundaries and resting initial state hold automatically, leaving the loss with only the interior equations of coupled electro-elastodynamics and the data misfit. Non-dimensional scaling brings all governing coefficients within one decade of O(1), and the setup removes the boundary and initial-condition penalty weights that soft-constraint methods must tune. In a six-way comparison (plane-strain PZT-5H, manufactured wavefield, 30 dB noise), a soft-penalty baseline with adaptive weights converges to an erroneous $e_{15}$ in four of the five runs (51.7% mean error), and fixed penalties reach an error of 0.85% only after a second-order optimization stage. The constrained formulations reach mean $e_{15}$ errors between 0.15% and 0.51% with held-out displacement errors below 1%. Within these variants, the spatial multiplier gives rapid first-order convergence, and the quadratic temporal multiplier lowers the early-time electrostatic residual by a factor of 6.8 versus a linear one. On finite-element data along one subsurface line, the full formulation recovers $e_{15}$ with 1.19% mean error at 30 dB and keeps it between 0.65% and 2.71% across a 40 to 0 dB noise sweep. Finally, training on displacements alone still recovers $e_{15}$ with mean errors of 0.45% on finite-element and 1.64% on manufactured data.

title: IDPForge: deep learning of proteins with global and local regions of disorder
abstract: Abstract Although machine learning has transformed protein structure prediction of folded protein ground states with remarkable accuracy, intrinsically disordered proteins and regions (IDPs/IDRs) are defined by diverse and dynamical structural ensembles that are predicted with low confidence by algorithms such as AlphaFold and RoseTTAFold. We present a machine learning method, IDPForge ( I ntrinsically D isordered P rotein, FO lded and disordered R egion GE nerator), that exploits a transformer protein language diffusion model to create all-atom IDP ensembles and IDR ensembles that maintains the folded domains. IDPForge does not require sequence-specific training, back transformations from coarse-grained representations, nor ensemble reweighting. The created IDP/IDR conformational ensembles show good agreement with both NMR and SAXS solution experimental data, and options for biasing with experimental restraints are available if desired. IDPForge with these diverse capabilities facilitates integrative and structural studies for proteins that contain intrinsic disorder, and is available as an open source resource for general use.

title: Hyperbolic Neural Operator
abstract: Neural operators have emerged as powerful surrogates for solving PDEs, significantly accelerating scientific computation. While transformer-based architectures offer unmatched flexibility for irregular domains, they suffer from a fundamental efficiency gap: standard attention mechanisms assign uniform interaction budgets to all token pairs, neglecting the physical reality that far-field interactions are often compressible. To address this mismatch, we draw inspiration from classical fast solvers that exploit hierarchical near-far decompositions. We further observe that embedding such tree-structured hierarchies in Euclidean space incurs inherent distortion, whereas hyperbolic space naturally accommodates exponential branching. Consequently, we propose \textbf{Hyperbolic Neural Operator (HNO)}, which leverages intrinsic hyperbolic geometry to instantiate a continuous Gibbs kernel based on stabilized geodesic distances on the Lorentz hyperboloid. This design imposes a geometric inductive bias that naturally enjoys robust multi-scale routing akin to the Fast Multipole Method (FMM), yet within a unified, learnable attention mechanism. Empirically, HNO achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on six PDE benchmarks and two large-scale unstructured CFD tasks, reducing the mean relative $\ell_2$ error by up to 40\% compared to leading baselines. Codes are attached and will be available online.

title: HybridOM: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Ocean Modeling with Efficient Spatial Downscaling
abstract: Global ocean modeling is vital for climate science but struggles to balance computational efficiency with accuracy. Traditional numerical solvers are accurate but computationally expensive, while pure deep learning approaches, though fast, often lack physical consistency and long-term stability. To address this, we introduce HybridOM, a framework integrating a lightweight, differentiable numerical solver as a skeleton to enforce physical laws, with a neural network as the flesh to correct subgrid-scale dynamics. To enable efficient high-resolution modeling, we further introduce a physics-informed regional downscaling mechanism based on flux gating. This design achieves the inference efficiency of AI-based methods while preserving the accuracy and robustness of physical models. Extensive experiments on the GLORYS12V1 and OceanBench dataset validate HybridOM's performance in two distinct regimes: long-term subseasonal-to-seasonal simulation and short-term operational forecasting coupled with the FuXi-2.0 weather model. Results demonstrate that HybridOM achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while maintaining physical consistency, offering a robust solution for next-generation ocean digital twins.

title: Hybrid Numerical PINNs: On the effectiveness of numerical differentiation for complex problems
abstract: Automatic differentiation (AD) is the default tool for computing physical derivatives in physics-informed models, but it faces significant limitations when applied to general frameworks, restricting their effectiveness on real-world problems. To overcome these challenges, we propose a hybrid approach that integrates traditional numerical solvers, such as the finite element method, within physics-informed deep learning. This framework enables the exact imposition of Dirichlet boundary conditions seamlessly, and efficiently addresses complex, non-analytic problems. The proposed approach is versatile, making it suitable for integration into any physics-informed model. Crucially, our hybrid gradient computation is up to two orders of magnitude faster than AD, as its computational cost remains unaffected by the underlying model's complexity. We validate the method on representative two and three-dimensional numerical examples and analyze the training dynamics of the hybrid framework.

title: Homology Features for X-Ray Hyperspectral Images Segmentation
abstract: Characterizing Multi-Energy X-ray Transmission (XRT) hyperspectral images presents significant challenges for traditional classification frameworks due to high-dimensional redundancy and non-linear spectral overlaps. Although manifold learning techniques such as UMAP enhance spectral representation by preserving non-linear correlations, they do not explicitly utilize the geometric structure of the embedded manifold for segmentation. This study introduces a hybrid architecture that integrates topological features derived from persistent homology with convolutional and graph neural networks. The approach computes Vietoris-Rips persistent homology on UMAP-projected superpixel point clouds to capture H 1 cyclic structures that encode spectral heterogeneity. These topological descriptors are combined with pixel-level CNN features through a broadcasting mechanism that propagates superpixel-level graph representations to full spatial resolution. Experimental results on XRT multi-energy imagery demonstrate that the proposed hybrid model significantly outperforms both CNN-only and superpixel-pooling fusion baselines, suggesting that topological features provide complementary discriminative information to local spectralspatial descriptors.
