title: Higher-Order Fourier Neural Operator: Explicit Mode Mixer for Nonlinear PDEs
abstract: Neural operators provide resolution-equivariant deep learning models for learning mappings between function spaces. Among them, the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) is particularly effective: its spectral convolution combines a low-dimensional Fourier representation with strong empirical performance, enabling generalization across resolutions. While this design aligns with settings where the Fourier basis diagonalizes the underlying operator, such as linear, constant-coefficient PDEs on periodic domains, in which Fourier modes evolve independently, nonlinear PDEs exhibit structured interactions between modes governed by polynomial nonlinearities. To capture this inductive bias, we introduce the **Higher-Order Spectral Convolution**, a spectral mixer that extends FNO from diagonal modulation to explicit $n$-linear mode mixing aligned with nonlinear PDE dynamics. Across benchmarks, including Burgers and Navier-Stokes equations, our method consistently improves accuracy in nonlinear regimes, achieving lower error while retaining the efficiency of FFT-based architectures.

title: High-fidelity training-free photovoltaic module mapping from multi-view UAV imagery
abstract: High-fidelity photovoltaic (PV) module mapping requires complete instance recovery and accurate delineation. Vision foundation models offer zero-shot segmentation, but converting incomplete and inconsistent predictions across views into a complete, geometrically accurate map of individual modules remains challenging. We propose the Multi-View PV Module Mapper (MV-PVMapper), a training-free framework coupling vision foundation models with unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) photogrammetry. First, Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) generates candidates from original images using text prompts. Their contours are then transferred into object space through per-module slope correction to limit distortion from surface-model noise, and verified against representative module dimensions to guide cross-view instance selection. Finally, accepted instances return to all covering images as box prompts for SAM~3, supplementing text prompts with spatial cues for iterative segmentation, verification and fusion. On five-direction surveys of three operational rooftop PV plants at approximately 1 cm nadir ground sampling distance, two feedback iterations recover 7,710 of 7,711 reference modules with no false positives at an intersection-over-union (IoU) matching threshold of 0.5. Macro-averaged area precision and recall reach 99.00 % and 98.52 %, respectively. Averaged across sites, the aggregated Jaccard index reaches 97.55 %, compared with 60.73 % and 41.24 % for orthomosaic segmentation and multi-view pixel-voting baselines, respectively; average precision at the stricter IoU threshold of 0.95 reaches 95.67 %. Ablation studies show that module-size constraints are critical for instance separation, while slope correction and feedback to all covering views improve boundary accuracy. These results are achieved without task-specific image annotation or segmentation-model weight updates.

title: High-fidelity quantum gate learning via physics-informed neural networks
abstract: We propose a physics-informed neural network (PINN) approach for high-fidelity quantum gate learning in both one- and two-qubit systems. We train a PINN using the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, where smooth control fields with fixed boundary conditions are obtained by minimizing a loss function that considers model dynamics, gate error, physical constraints, regularization terms, and multiple initial conditions. Training considers pairs of mutually unbiased bases, while independent validation combines Haar-random input states with the average gate fidelity. Unitary simulations yield an average gate infidelity of $8.49\times10^{-8}$ for Hadamard and values between $3.39\times10^{-7}$ and $4.96\times10^{-6}$ for controlled-NOT under $XX$, $YY$, and $ZZ$ interactions. We examine how the learned control fields depend on the coupling, training configuration, and available local fields, including five exchange-type dipolar scenarios. We test the learned control fields under the Lindblad master equation with dephasing and amplitude damping, theoretically reproducing the expected first-order fidelity loss in the weak-dissipation regime. Finally, boundary-adapted Chebyshev expansions represent 139 learned controls with a minimum common count of $K_\ast=24$ coefficients per control for all eleven family-averaged mean squared errors to fall below $10^{-6}$. Separately, square-pulse and Strang propagation at $K=30$ preserve all 31 continuous polynomial references within infidelity $10^{-5}$ at $N=128$ and all larger tested resolutions, under both sampling rules. These results connect multi-state gate synthesis, control-resource characterization, and compact square-pulse playback.

title: High-Resolution Quantitative MRI Using Contrast-Domain Multiscale Energy (MuSE) Regularization
abstract: Quantitative MRI methods can offer tissue parameter maps (e.g. T1) that are comparable across scanners, sessions and subjects, together with multiple contrast-weighted images from a single scan. However, most data are acquired at 1 mm, which limits their use in neurodegenerative diseases that affect fine brain structures. We introduce, to our knowledge, the first diffusion-model-based reconstruction for quantitative MRI at 0.5 mm isotropic resolution from scans of less than 5 minutes, which has eightfold smaller voxel volume than clinical protocols. The key idea is to apply the prior to the synthesized contrast images rather than to the subspace coefficients. The prior is then independent of the temporal basis and the sequence, which improves generalization and allows a 2-D multiscale energy (MuSE) model trained on grayscale CelebA face images to be used without any MRI training data. The explicit energy makes reconstruction MAP estimation by a step-size-free majorize-minimize algorithm that regularizes a rotating subset of contrasts along different axes, which makes 3-D multi-contrast reconstruction tractable. For 3-D radial MPnRAGE at 7 T in 4.3 min, MuSE reduced the phantom NRMSE from 0.133 (CG-SENSE) and 0.091 (L1-wavelet) to 0.074 and the WM T1 interquartile range from 117 and 47 ms to 38 ms, and it was demonstrated in vivo at 7 T.

title: Hierarchical Causal Abduction: A Foundation Framework for Explainable Model Predictive Control
abstract: Model Predictive Control (MPC) is widely used to operate safety-critical infrastructure by predicting future trajectories and optimizing control actions. However, nonlinear dynamics, hard safety constraints, and numerical optimization often render individual control moves opaque to human operators, undermining trust and hindering deployment. This paper presents Hierarchical Causal Abduction (HCA), which combines (i) physics-informed reasoning via domain knowledge graphs, (ii) optimization evidence from Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) multipliers, and (iii) temporal causal discovery via the PCMCI algorithm to generate faithful, human-interpretable explanations for control actions computed by nonlinear MPC. Across three diverse control applications (greenhouse climate, building HVAC, chemical process engineering) with expert validation, HCA improves explanation accuracy by 53\% over LIME (0.478 vs. 0.311) using a single set of cross-domain parameters without per-domain tuning; domain-specific KKT-threshold calibration over 2--3 days further increases accuracy to 0.88. Ablation studies confirm that each evidence source is essential, with 32--37\% accuracy degradation when any component is removed, and HCA's ranking-and-validation methodology generalizes beyond MPC to other prediction-based decision systems, including learning-based control and trajectory planning.

title: Helix: Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning for Open-Ended Scientific Problem Solving
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) with reasoning abilities have demonstrated growing promise for tackling complex scientific problems. Yet such tasks are inherently domain-specific, unbounded and open-ended, demanding exploration across vast and flexible solution spaces. Existing approaches, whether purely learning-based or reliant on carefully designed workflows, often suffer from limited exploration efficiency and poor generalization. To overcome these challenges, we present **HELIX**---a **H**ierarchical **E**volutionary reinforcement **L**earning framework with **I**n-context e**X**periences. HELIX introduces two key novelties: (i) a diverse yet high-quality pool of candidate solutions that broadens exploration through in-context learning, and (ii) reinforcement learning for iterative policy refinement that progressively elevates solution quality. This synergy enables the discovery of more advanced solutions. On the circle packing task, HELIX achieves state-of-the-art result with a sum of radii of 2.63598308 using only a 14B model. Across standard machine learning benchmarks, HELIX further surpasses GPT-4o with a carefully engineered pipeline, delivering an average F1 improvement of 5.95 points on the Adult and Bank Marketing datasets.

title: Heavy-tailed Physics-Informed Neural Networks
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) enforce physical laws by minimizing partial differential equation (PDE) residuals and auxiliary constraints. Standard training relies on a mean-squared error (MSE) objective, which implicitly assumes independent Gaussian residuals with a fixed global variance. We show theoretically and empirically that residuals encountered during PINN training are heterogeneous and heavy-tailed, revealing a systematic mismatch with this assumption. As a consequence, a small number of large residuals can disproportionately dominate both the loss and gradient, leading to poorly balanced optimization dynamics. Motivated by this mismatch, we adopt a Student-$t$ residual model to explicitly capture heavy-tailed behavior. An equivalent hierarchical representation yields an expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm that alternates between estimating residual-dependent weights and optimizing network parameters via a weighted MSE objective, allowing existing PINN solvers to be reused in the M-step. The resulting training dynamics bound the influence of extreme residuals and admit almost sure convergence guarantees under standard stochastic optimization assumptions. Experiments across a diverse suite of challenging PDE benchmarks demonstrate consistently improved solution accuracy and robustness compared to standard PINN training.

title: Harmonized Cone for Feasible and Non-conflict Directions in Training Physics-Informed Neural Networks
abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for solving PDEs, yet training is difficult due to a multi-objective loss that couples PDE residuals, initial/boundary conditions, and auxiliary physics terms. Existing remedies often yield infeasible scaling factors or conflicting update directions, resulting in degraded performance. In this paper, we show that training PINNs requires jointly considering feasible scaling factors and a non-conflict direction. Through a geometric analysis of per-loss gradients, we define the $\textit{harmonized cone}$ as the intersection of their primal and dual cones, which characterizes directions that are simultaneously feasible and non-conflicting. Building on this, we propose $HARMONIC$ (HARMONIzed Cone gradient descent), a training procedure that computes updates within the harmonized cone by leveraging the Double Description method to aggregate extreme rays. Theoretically, we establish convergence guarantees in nonconvex settings and prove the existence of a nontrivial harmonized cone. Across standard PDE benchmarks, $HARMONIC$ generally outperforms state-of-the-art methods while ensuring feasible and non-conflict updates.

title: Hardware Demonstration of Neural-Surrogated Quantum-Enhanced MCMC for Large-Scale Constrained Boltzmann Sampling
abstract: Neural-surrogated quantum-enhanced Markov chain Monte Carlo (QeMCMC) uses neural networks trained on samples from the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) to accelerate Boltzmann sampling. A divide-and-conquer strategy extends this approach to larger systems, but independently optimizing QAOA parameters for each subproblem is costly. In this paper, we develop a hardware-efficient implementation of neural-surrogated QeMCMC and demonstrate it using an IBM Quantum Heron r2 processor. Experiments with $N=144$ binary variables reveal faster autocorrelation decay for appropriate subproblem sizes while exposing challenges in neural-surrogate learning for larger blocks. We then extend the demonstration to a system with $N=1064$, where the autocorrelation decay rate per MCMC step is approximately $5.2$ and $12.3$ times those of global and local Kawasaki dynamics, respectively. These results demonstrate faster autocorrelation decay in a system exceeding one thousand variables using samples generated on quantum hardware.

title: Hard Constraint Projection in a Physics Informed Neural Network (Burgers)
abstract: Physics informed machine learning provides a framework to study and simulate fluid dynamics, potentially at a fraction of the computational cost of traditional numerical methods, with the goal of improving the explainability, accuracy and robustness of purely data driven machine learning methods. In this work, we extend the hard constraint projection (HCP) method developed by Chen et al. [Journal of Computational Physics, 445, 110624, 2021] from a linear partial differential equation (PDE) to a nonlinear PDE: the 1D Burgers' equation. To strictly impose a discrete approximation of the governing equation, the Burgers' equation is first locally discretised (using a finite difference stencil) then decomposed into a constraint matrix and a prediction matrix. Using tools from linear algebra, the constraint matrix is used to construct a projection matrix. A physics informed neural network (PINN) [Raissi et al. Journal of Computational Physics, 378, 686, 2019] is used to predict the velocity, and a final unlearnable layer projects the velocity prediction to the hyperplane of exact solutions to a discretised form of the Burgers' equation. Our initial results indicate that the HCP-PINN initially trains similarly to an equivalent PINN, and as the PINN loss plateaus, the HCP-PINN loss continues to decline. When tested on a previously unseen uniform grid of points covering the domain, the HCP-PINN exhibits higher accuracy, converging to a data error approximately an order of magnitude lower than the comparable PINN. We also observe that the inclusion of the HCP layer results in better observance of the governing PDE. Our findings suggest that the HCP-PINN can be more robust to the selection of physics collocation points, and less dependent on collocation point quantity.

title: HamFormer: A Hamiltonian Flow-based SE(3)-Transformer for Conformation Optimization
abstract: The Transformer architecture plays a central role in modern deep learning, and its SE(3)-equivariant variants have been widely applied to molecular conformation modeling and optimization. Given its importance, many methods attempt to interpret and improve the Transformer through the lens of dynamics. However, they mainly focus on a single attention head rather than the full Transformer architecture and seldom consider SE(3)-equivariance in their proposed models. In this study, we propose an improved SE(3)-Transformer architecture, called HamFormer, which revisits the design of SE(3)-Transformer through the lens of Hamiltonian flow. In particular, we define a parametrized Hamiltonian flow in the phase space of position and velocity, corresponding to optimizing an energy functional that combines an optimal transport-based potential with a damped momentum. The Lie-Trotter splitting framework of the Hamiltonian flow leads to the proposed HamFormer architecture, whose feedforward computation achieves the optimization step of the proposed energy functional. Furthermore, we combine HamFormer with Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN), build a new model for molecular conformation optimization. Extensive experiments on molecular ground-state conformation prediction show that HamFormer provides a strong and physically interpretable surrogate for classic SE(3)-Transformer and generally outperforms state-of-the-art competitors.

title: Guided and Interpretable Neural Operator Design for Partial Differential Equation Learning
abstract: Accurate numerical solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) are crucial in numerous science and engineering applications. In this work, we introduce a novel neural PDE solver named AFDONet, which incorporates neural operator learning and adaptive Fourier decomposition (AFD) theory for the first time into a specifically designed variational autoencoder (VAE) structure, to solve a general class of nonlinear PDEs on smooth manifolds. AFDONet is the first neural PDE solver whose architectural and component design is fully guided by an established mathematical framework (in this case, AFD theory), turning neural operator design from an art to a science. Thus, AFDONet also exhibits exceptional mathematical explainability and groundness, and enjoys several desired properties. Furthermore, AFDONet achieves outstanding solution accuracy and competitive computational efficiency in several benchmark problems. In particular, thanks to its deep connections with AFD theory, AFDONet shows superior performance in solving PDEs on i) arbitrary (Riemannian) manifolds, and ii) datasets with sharp gradients. Overall, this work presents a new paradigm for designing explainable neural operator frameworks.

title: Guaranteeing Conservation of Integrals with Projection in Physics-Informed Neural Networks
abstract: We propose a novel projection method that guarantees the conservation of integral quantities in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). While the soft constraint PINNs use to enforce the structure of partial differential equations (PDEs) enables necessary flexibility during training, it also permits the discovered solution to violate physical laws. To address this, we introduce a projection method that guarantees the conservation of the linear and quadratic integrals, both separately and jointly. We derived the projection formulae by solving constrained non-linear optimization problems and found that our PINN modified with the projection, which we call PINN-Proj, reduced the error in the conservation of these quantities by three to four orders of magnitude compared to the soft constraint and marginally reduced the error in the PDE solution. We also found evidence that the projection improved convergence through improving the conditioning of the loss landscape. Our method holds promise as a general framework to guarantee the conservation of any integral quantity in a PINN if a projection is found and is tractable in neural network training.

title: Grounding LLMs in Scientific Discovery via Embodied Actions
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown significant potential in scientific discovery but struggle to bridge the gap between theoretical reasoning and verifiable physical simulation. Existing solutions operate in a passive "execute-then-response" loop and thus lack runtime perception, obscuring agents to transient anomalies (e.g., numerical instability or diverging oscillations). To address this limitation, we propose EmbodiedAct, a framework that transforms established scientific software into active embodied agents by grounding LLMs in embodied actions with a tight perception-execution loop. We instantiate EmbodiedAct within MATLAB and evaluate it on complex engineering design and scientific modeling tasks. Extensive experiments show that EmbodiedAct significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving SOTA performance by ensuring satisfactory reliability and stability in long-horizon simulations and enhanced accuracy in scientific modeling.

title: Ground-Wing: A Parametric 3D Wing-in-Ground-Effect Dataset for Benchmarking Neural Surrogate Models
abstract: This paper presents a CFD dataset of a highly parametrized 3D wing operating in ground effect, designed for benchmarking neural surrogate models for aerodynamic prediction, using a wing shape and flow conditions typically encountered in motorsport applications. The dataset comprises 770 RANS simulations of 194 unique wing configurations, sampled across 27 airfoil profile variants and 4 distances from the ground, spanning variations in wing sweep, chord, taper, angle of attack, and tip twist. Six neural network architectures representing distinct paradigms --- convolutional (DoMINO), graph-based (X-MeshGraphNet), transformer-based (AB-UPT, GeoTransolver, GAOT), and JEPA-based (AeroJEPA) --- are evaluated on their ability to predict surface pressure coefficient and wall shear stress distributions, from which integral drag and lift coefficients are recovered. The dataset is intended to be used as a challenging benchmark for surrogate CFD models, due to the uniqueness of the ground effect being absent from other wing and airfoil datasets.

title: Greenscapes: Optimized Vegetation Configurations in Cities
abstract: Vegetation plays a central role in cities, serving functional roles such as balancing shade and sky exposure, shaping the microclimate, carbon sequestration, and providing acoustic screening. Furthermore, aesthetic choices in landscape styles (formal, modernist, picturesque) are important for citizens' well-being and should be considered in the design of urban landscapes. In this paper, we present a novel method for placing vegetation, ranging from shrubs to large trees, in 3D urban scenes. Our method uses individual lots as input and employs a conditioned Vision-Language Model (VLM) to generate a top-down rendering of vegetation, placing large trees, small trees, and shrubs on lawn areas. This rendering is then converted into a 3D scene by detecting individual plants and selecting appropriate 3D assets. To refine the proposed configurations, we define an optimization loop that keeps the VLM-generated positions fixed after a deterministic feasibility repair and uses CMA-ES to optimize per-instance scale transformations along with discrete vegetation asset substitutions. To define the objective function for the optimization, we evaluate the generated 3D scenes with efficient surrogate models of shade and path-based acoustic exposure. Furthermore, we render in-scene views at each optimization step to compute view-dependent perceptual descriptors, enabling the generation of both aesthetic and functional vegetation layouts for urban scenes.

title: Gravity-induced branch selection and no-shear theorems for compressible pure-swirl vortices
abstract: We classify steady axisymmetric pure-swirl solutions of the compressible Navier–Stokes–Fourier equations for a calorically perfect ideal gas under uniform gravity, with no distributed volumetric heating or azimuthal body forcing. Radial and vertical momentum balance impose the compatibility conditions T=Θ(χ) and p=P(χ), where χ=gz−Ψ(r) and Ψ′(r)=Vϕ2/r. For constant dynamic viscosity and arbitrary positive conductivity k(T), the azimuthal momentum equation admits Vϕ=Ar+B/r, but the energy equation retains only the two pure branches: Ar with uniform temperature and B/r with k(T)Tχ=−2μ. The mixed branch AB≠0 is excluded. If viscosity depends on temperature, every sheared region must satisfy μ[T(χ)]=μ0eλχ. Power-law and Sutherland viscosity under the standard constant-Prandtl closure are incompatible with the remaining energy constraint; no steady sheared pure-swirl state then exists in this class. The constant-viscosity potential branch survives as an exact conductive solution on an annulus. Thus, each additional thermodynamic or transport constraint reduces the admissible pure-swirl solution set.

title: Graph-Based Operator Learning from Limited Data on Irregular Domains
abstract: Operator learning seeks to approximate mappings from input functions to output solutions, particularly in the context of partial differential equations (PDEs). While recent advances such as DeepONet and Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) have demonstrated strong performance, they often rely on regular grid discretizations, limiting their applicability to complex or irregular domains. In this work, we propose a Graph-based Operator Learning with Attention (GOLA) framework that addresses this limitation by constructing graphs from irregularly sampled spatial points and leveraging attention-enhanced Graph Neural Netwoks (GNNs) to model spatial dependencies with global information. To improve the expressive capacity, we introduce a Fourier-based encoder that projects input functions into a frequency space using learnable complex coefficients, allowing for flexible embeddings even with sparse or nonuniform samples. We evaluated our approach across a range of 2D PDEs, including Darcy Flow, Advection, Eikonal, and Nonlinear Diffusion, under varying sampling densities. Our method consistently outperforms baselines, particularly in data-scarce regimes, demonstrating strong generalization and efficiency on irregular domains.

title: Graph Rewiring based on Flow Alignment for Improving Fluid Simulation
abstract: To overcome the computational burden of traditional computational fluid dynamics (CFD), graph neural network-based (GNN) learned simulators have attracted growing interest because they naturally operate on CFD meshes. However, classical GNNs only exchange information between neighbouring nodes, limiting flow prediction accuracy. While graph rewiring can improve information propagation, existing methods are mostly designed for generic graphs, and PIORF relies on long-range connections for fluid simulation. In this work, we show that simply connecting all 2-hop nodes can already achieve competitive performance with PIORF, raising questions about the necessity of distant rewiring. Motivated by fluid transport principles, we propose Flow Alignment Rewiring (FLARE), a simple and efficient local rewiring method that connects 2-hop nodes only when their relative direction aligns with the input flow direction. Hence, FLARE is a physics-informed local rewiring method, different from PIORF and well-aligned with fluid physics. Extensive numerical experiments on flows over a cylinder, single-, and tandem-airfoil under different flow conditions and deep network architectures demonstrate that FLARE outperforms PIORF and various 2-hop rewiring approaches by a significant margin.

title: Graph Mamba Operator for Learning the Dynamics of Particle-based Systems
abstract: Modelling complex 3D dynamics---from molecular conformations to particle interactions and human motion---requires capturing dependencies spanning long temporal horizons and non-local spatial interactions. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have shown promise in spatio-temporal settings but often suffer from instability and degraded accuracy in long-range forecasting. We propose the Graph Mamba Operator (GraMO), a neural operator that integrates state-space models (SSMs) with geometric learning to capture spatio-temporal correlations jointly. To jointly model complex dynamics, GraMO integrates a stable, SSM-based temporal backbone with an SSM-parameterized graph update to capture long-range spatial dependencies. Unlike stepwise predictors that accumulate errors over time, GraMO learns entire trajectories in a single forward pass. Across diverse benchmarks ranging from molecular dynamics to human motion capture, GraMO shows notable improvements in trajectory fidelity, stability, and robustness over strong baselines with relative improvements of over 26.3\% on motion capture benchmarks and 25.2\% on MD17 final-state prediction. Ablation studies reveal that temporal SSM components consistently improve performance, while spatial SSM updates show task-dependent benefits---helping with long-range interactions in large molecules but potentially hindering performance on systems with primarily local dependencies. Altogether, these results suggest that selective integration of SSM components with graph neural networks can improve performance on particle-based systems, with applications in molecular simulations, articulated rigid body dynamics, and particle systems.

title: Graph Foundation Models Can Become Effective Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detectors
abstract: Multivariate time series anomaly detection (MTSAD) relies on modeling both temporal dynamics and inter-sensor dependencies to identify complex system faults. Although graph-based detectors explicitly model sensor topologies, they train task-specific networks from scratch on limited target-domain data, remaining vulnerable to spurious correlations and unable to reuse transferable priors. While pretrained Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) offer transferable topological priors and anomaly discriminability, directly adapting them to MTSAD is hindered by cross-modal feature-topology mismatch, unreliable pseudo-anomaly supervision, and decision distortion during node-to-window aggregation. To fill these gaps, we propose a novel adaptation framework, Gfm4Mtsad, which unleashes pretrained GFMs for MTSAD. We introduce the Structure-and-Information Contract Alignment (SICA) module to bridge continuous time series and the pretrained GFM space. This module harmonizes principal subspace token projection, normal-prior-guided graph construction, and residual recovery to suppress spurious edges while retaining fine-grained temporal details. We propose a Mechanism-Aligned Pseudo-Anomaly Screening strategy (MAPS) to steer unsupervised learning. It applies localized dependency breaks while preserving empirical residuals, selecting hard negatives near the normal boundary for targeted supervision. We develop a Tail-Gated Evidence Calibration mechanism (TGEC) to eliminate node-to-window aggregation distortion. It calibrates multi-granular graph responses against normal operational references, strictly preserving benign score rankings while selectively refining extreme anomaly candidates in the tail distribution for reliable window detection and interpretable sensor evidence. Extensive evaluations with two GFM backbones demonstrate that Gfm4Mtsad achieves superior detection performance over existing baselines.
summary: Multivariate time series anomaly detection (MTSAD) relies on modeling both temporal dynamics and inter-sensor dependencies to identify complex system faults. Although graph-based detectors explicitly model sensor topologies, they train task-specific networks from scratch on limited target-domain data, remaining vulnerable to spurious correlations and unable to reuse transferable priors. While pretrained Graph Founda…

title: Global Existence for a Drift-Diffusion Model of Electrical Discharge in MEMS
abstract: We study a coupled elliptic-parabolic system modelling electrical discharge in a micro-electro-mechanical (MEMS) capacitor: a Poisson equation for the electrostatic potential, coupled to drift-diffusion equations for the ion and electron densities with a Townsend ionization source whose rate per electron grows linearly in the electric field. Gimperlein, He and Lacey proved local well-posedness and left open whether the densities blow up in finite time. We first prove a continuation criterion in a weak norm: a finite-time singularity forces the space charge to be unbounded in H^1_D, the dual of the space of H^1 functions vanishing on the electrodes, so blow-up cannot be quasi-neutral. We then exclude it altogether when the two diffusivities coincide and the vacuum field is bounded: the weak solution is then global in time. To our knowledge this is the first global existence result without smallness assumptions for a drift-diffusion-Poisson model of gas discharge whose ionization rate is unbounded in the field. The proof uses the electrostatic energy and the number of carriers in place of the usual free energy: the ionization source cancels in the energy balance, the Joule heating is dissipative, and the two quantities close through a linear Gronwall inequality. Numerical experiments on a discharge in a micrometre gap, with the Townsend constants and the mobilities of air, provide evidence for the extension to unequal diffusivities and bear on the existence of a breakdown threshold.

title: Geometric Laplace Neural Operator
abstract: Neural operators have emerged as powerful tools for learning mappings between function spaces, enabling efficient solutions to partial differential equations across varying inputs and domains. Despite the success, existing methods often struggle with non-periodic excitations, transient responses, and signals defined on irregular or non-Euclidean geometries. To address this, we propose a generalized operator learning framework based on a pole–residue decomposition enriched with exponential basis functions, enabling expressive modeling of aperiodic and decaying dynamics. Building on this formulation, we introduce the Geometric Laplace Neural Operator (GLNO), which embeds the Laplace spectral representation into the eigen-basis of the Laplace–Beltrami operator, extending operator learning to arbitrary Riemannian manifolds without requiring periodicity or uniform grids. We further design a grid-invariant network architecture (GLNONet) that realizes GLNO in practice. Extensive experiments on PDEs/ODEs and real-world datasets demonstrate our robust performance over other state-of-the-art models.

title: GeoSim: Benchmarking Multi-Field Neural Operators for Geodynamics
abstract: Learning reliable surrogates for geodynamic models requires benchmarks that resolve coupled fields and temporal stability. We present GeoSim, a benchmark of high-resolution two-dimensional mantle-plume simulations generated with I2VIS, comprising 237 trajectories across two parameter regimes, with six coupled fields, physical timestamps, and trajectory-level splits. GeoSim defines short-window prediction and autonomous rollout, and evaluates representative neural operators field by field. Across models, we observe a pronounced scalar--velocity gap: scalar fields are reconstructed accurately while velocity errors remain large, and short-window accuracy does not imply stable rollout. We also evaluate MFGNO (Multi-Field Graph Neural Operator), a joint multi-field graph baseline designed for this benchmark; on GeoSim-Plume1, under a fixed per-field objective, it reduces horizontal and vertical velocity errors by 58.4% and 38.5% relative to an independent-field graph baseline, while an explicit field-difference input shows no measurable benefit at this scale. GeoSim provides a reproducible benchmark for field-wise diagnosis and long-horizon evaluation of geodynamic surrogates.

title: GeoCMON: Operator Learning on Deformable Domains via Disentangled Geometric Conditioning
abstract: Partial differential equations (PDEs) defined on non-rigid, parametrically vary- ing domains with heterogeneous boundary conditions pose significant computa- tional challenges for classical numerical solvers due to repeated discretizations and costly simulations. Operator learning frameworks offer promising surrogate modeling approaches that approximate solution operators mapping domain and boundary parameters directly to solution fields without explicit meshing. How- ever, existing neural operator architectures struggle with input modality entan- glement, training instability, and limited generalization on highly deformable ge- ometries with complex boundary inputs. To address these limitations, we intro- duce GeoCMON, a Geometric-Conditioned Multi-Branch Operator Network that explicitly disentangles geometric and boundary features via specialized encod- ing branches, which are fused with a spatial trunk network through element-wise multiplication and Einstein summation to enable expressive conditioning. We aug- ment the architecture with conditional residual connections within branches to en- hance gradient flow and training stability, and adopt a weighted mean squared error loss emphasizing regions of physically significant solution magnitude to prioritize challenging prediction regimes. Comprehensive empirical evaluations on parametric PDE datasets derived from 2D Laplace problems demonstrate that GeoCMON substantially outperforms baseline multi-branch methods, achieving superior accuracy across stratified difficulty bins, improved training dynamics ev- idenced by higher synchronization scores and reduced activation variance, and enhanced feature orthogonality indicative of robust representation. Gradient noise analyses confirm that these gains do not compromise optimization stability. Col- lectively, our contributions advance scalable and interpretable operator learning for PDEs on complex, deformable domains, providing a principled architectural and methodological framework for surrogate modeling in scientific computing.

title: Generative Neural Operators through Diffusion Last Layer
abstract: Neural operators provide a powerful framework for learning discretization invariant mappings between function spaces, but standard deterministic models do not capture predictive uncertainty. We introduce *diffusion last layer* (DLL), a modular probabilistic output head for neural operator backbones. DLL represents target fields through an input dependent low rank expansion inspired by the Karhunen--Lo\`eve expansion and learns a conditional diffusion model over the corresponding coefficient space. This design enables efficient distributional modeling while preserving the structural advantages of operator learning. On stochastic PDE benchmarks with random forcing, DLL achieves strong distributional fidelity and performs competitively with pixel space and conventional latent diffusion baselines. In deterministic long horizon rollout tasks, DLL improves rollout stability over the underlying backbone and provides useful estimates of predictive uncertainty under compounding autoregressive errors. These results suggest that diffusion modeling in learned coefficient spaces offers a practical route to uncertainty aware neural operators. Code is available at https://github.com/sungwpark/dll-no

title: Generative Design and Graph Neural Network Screening of Novel Bimetallic Alloy Catalysts for the Hydrogen Evolution Reaction
abstract: Identifying earth-abundant catalysts for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is a central challenge in scalable green hydrogen production. We present a computational pipeline that couples diffusion-based generative modelling, machine-learning force-field relaxation, and graph neural network (GNN) property prediction to discover bimetallic HER catalysts beyond the structures and stoichiometries covered by existing adsorption databases. A generative model (MatterGen) is fine-tuned on bulk alloy structures labelled with their minimum hydrogen adsorption energy and steered towards adsorption energies near zero. From the generated pool we retain the stable structures that are novel bimetallic alloys: binary compositions built from the training-set metals but at stoichiometries or structures absent from that database. Each candidate's low-index facets are ranked by a machine-learning-force-field (MatterSim) surface-energy screen, and only the most stable terminations are converted into explicit slab models with hydrogen adsorbed at all high-symmetry surface sites and relaxed with the same force field. Two GNN surrogates (MEGNet and ALIGNN), trained on a high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) dataset, then screen the resulting slab candidates. Because the two models encode the local environment through different inductive biases, we retain only the alloys on which both agree, reducing the influence of any single model. This consensus screening, combined with a MatterSim energy-difference triangulation, resulted in a shortlist of near-thermoneutral bimetallic candidates. Eight are validated with plane-wave DFT, and four of them, Pd5Au, Pt5Rh, Cu5Pt3, and Pd13Ru3, bind hydrogen within the thermoneutral window. All eight alloys are dynamically stable by phonon calculations. These four alloys are highlighted as DFT-validated bimetallic HER candidates for experimental follow-up.

title: Generalizing Multi-Scale Time-Series Modeling with a Single Operator
abstract: Multi-scale modeling has emerged as an effective design principle for time-series forecasting by capturing temporal dynamics at multiple resolutions. As no principled foundation has been established in the literature, we unify existing scaling methods into a scaling operator family, revealing a fundamental limitation of existing approaches: reliance on fixed and discrete scaling. To address this limitation, we propose SiGMA (Single Generalized Multi-scale Architecture), which enables distance-aware scaling via the learnable discrete Gaussian (LDG) kernel grounded in scale-space theory. We evaluate SiGMA comprehensively on long- and short-term forecasting benchmarks against state-of-the-art multi-scale baselines. SiGMA outperforms all competitors on both tasks, especially achieving the best performance in 13 out of 16 long-term evaluation settings. Beyond accuracy, SiGMA significantly improves training speed by up to 5.3 times and reduces memory consumption by up to 3.8 times over the strongest competitors. Code is available at https://github.com/cheonwoolee/SiGMA.

title: Generalized Spherical Neural Operators: Green’s Function Formulation
abstract: Neural operators offer powerful approaches for solving parametric partial differential equations, but extending them to spherical domains remains challenging due to the need to preserve intrinsic geometry while avoiding distortions that break rotational consistency. Existing spherical operators rely on rotational equivariance but often lack the flexibility for real-world complexity. We propose a generalized operator-design framework based on designable Green’s function and its harmonic expansion, establishing a solid operator-theoretic foundation for spherical learning. Based on this, we propose an absolute and relative position-dependent Green’s function that enables flexible balance of equivariance and invariance for real-world modeling. The resulting operator, Green's-function Spherical Neural Operator (GSNO) with a novel spectral learning method, can adapt to non-equivariant systems while retaining spherical geometry, spectral efficiency and grid invariance. To exploit GSNO, we develop SHNet, a hierarchical architecture that combines multi-scale spectral modeling with spherical up-down sampling, enhancing global feature representation. Evaluations on diffusion MRI, shallow water dynamics, and global weather forecasting, GSNO and SHNet consistently outperform state-of-the-art methods. The theoretical and experimental results position GSNO as a principled and generalized framework for spherical operator learning, bridging rigorous theory with real-world complexity. The code is available at: https://github.com/haot2025/GSNO.

title: Fusing Earth observation embeddings and spaceborne terrain with meteorological forcing for flood peak depth prediction from high-water marks
abstract: Flood peak depth on normally dry land governs damage and risk to life, but is observed only sparsely, by post-event high-water mark (HWM) surveys, and depth derived from satellite flood extent is produced after the event and inherits the vertical error of the digital elevation model (DEM) it is computed from. Deep-learning flood models have in turn been trained on hydrodynamic simulations rather than on observed depths. We ask whether flood peak depth can be learned from field observations and predicted before the peak from spaceborne terrain, geospatial foundation-model embeddings and antecedent meteorological forcing. We assembled 5689 USGS HWM surveys from 39 events (2011-2025) in 24 U.S. states and Puerto Rico, assigned each a peak time from nearby sensors, paired each with a rain-free window at the same site, and linked them to Copernicus GLO-30 terrain, AlphaEarth embeddings and 144 h of hourly forcing masked to the lead time. A cross-modal fusion network trained on these observations predicts depth at the surveyed marks with a mean absolute error of 0.39 m 6 h ahead of the peak. Supervision by surveyed depth corrects the DEM error implicitly: differencing the measured peak water level with the same DEM gives 0.93 m at the same marks, 2.4 times larger, although it uses the measured water level and the model does not. Forcing accounts for 77% of the attributed reduction in depth error; terrain and the embeddings are statistically equivalent to each other and contribute the remaining 23%. On eleven held-out events the model still separates flooded from rain-free conditions but no longer resolves depth at the marks (R2 = 0.03), so the skill reported here is confined to the events and regions sampled. Field-surveyed depths can thus supervise flood depth prediction and correct terrain error that extent-based estimation cannot, while transfer to unseen storms remains the open problem.

title: From crown splash to bell-shaped closure: Dynamics of laser-induced splashing on the liquid metal surface
abstract: This study combines high-speed imaging and multi-physics coupled numerical simulations to investigate the dynamic evolution and topological transition of free-surface splashing of Galinstan induced by nanosecond pulsed lasers. Within laser energies of 0.15–0.45 mJ and pulse durations of 150–350 ns, three sequential splashing regimes are observed experimentally with increasing laser pulse energy: open crown, transitional state, and closed bell-shaped crown. The fully closed crown with a steady central liquid column is reported for the first time in laser-induced liquid metal splashing. A compressible volume of fluid model accounting for vapor recoil pressure is established and validated against experiments. Flow-field analysis reveals that gas-phase recirculation vortices originating from the initial crater and pressure difference across the cavity dominate crown closure. A two-dimensional regime map is constructed using the crater aspect ratio γ* at laser pulse termination and equivalent Weber number We as coordinates. A simplified crater-liquid-film mechanical model is developed based on axisymmetric bell theory, yielding a critical criterion for bell-shaped closure. The theoretically predicted regime boundaries are qualitatively consistent with the experimental regime map. Furthermore, control experiments under oxygen-free environments are also conducted to verify the robustness of the regime map. This study provides mechanistic insights and a quantitative classification framework for topological transitions in laser-triggered liquid metal splashing.

title: From WSIs to Bulk, Spatial and Single-Cell Transcriptomics via Multi-Scale Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Understanding the spatial distribution of gene expression is key to studying complex diseases like cancer. While Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) and Single-Cell Transcriptomics (scT) provide high-resolution insights, they remain expensive and scarce. In contrast, standard histopathology Whole-Slide Images (WSIs) paired with bulk RNA sequencing are widely available. This work introduces a Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network (GNN) capable of simultaneously predicting bulk, spatial, and single-cell transcriptomics directly from WSIs. By extracting morphological features using a Pathology Foundation Model (PFM) (UNI2-h) and constructing spatial graphs at both patch and cell levels, the model learns the hierarchical relationships within the tissue. The network is trained on a combined dataset of The Cancer Genome Atlas Program (TCGA), Visium, and Xenium samples across lung, kidney, and breast tissues. A hybrid training strategy is employed, leveraging direct supervision alongside weakly supervised consistency losses to ensure predictions align across biological scales. Results show the model accurately predicts gene expression at the slide level and moderately at the patch level (strongest on Xenium), and achieves moderate correlation at the challenging single-cell level. Furthermore, downstream tasks explore the clinical relevance of these predictions, demonstrating their utility in survival analysis, spatial hazard mapping, and tumor classification via molecular signatures.

title: From Numerical Solvers to Graph Surrogates: Physics-Informed Losses for Data-Efficient CFD Modeling
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNN) represent a promising method for creating robust and physically interpretable surrogate models for fluid dynamics. These surrogates offer a significant advantage over traditional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solvers based on numerical methods because they require much less computational cost. In a GNN designed as a surrogate model for spatio-temporal partial differential equations, message passing can be interpreted as the propagation of physical quantities such as velocity, pressure, and temperature. The complexity of the Navier-Stokes equations, however, can limit the generalizability of existing models and lead to long training times. We show that including a physics-informed loss function based on the numerical methods used to generate the training data, specifically the finite volume method, can reduce the amount of data needed to train an accurate physics-informed surrogate compared with a purely data-driven baseline. By reducing the dataset size by 20\% and applying this approach, we achieved a 33\% reduction in convergence time. For larger datasets, model accuracy improved by up to 7.4\% within the same timeframe. Our method also avoids interpolation between cell centers and vertices, which can introduce errors from numerical discretization. Applying this soft constraint during training can support the development of future CFD surrogate GNN models that perform well even with smaller datasets.

title: From Natural Images to Medical Scans: Transferability of Diffusion Models for Medical Image Generation
abstract: Transfer learning from natural images is standard in supervised and increasingly adopted in self-supervised medical image analysis, but its role in generative modelling, and in particular diffusion denoisers, remains underexplored. Medical diffusion models typically train the denoiser from scratch, with no systematic evaluation of natural-image transfer. We analyse this across latent and pixel paradigms, model sizes (131M-952M) and two radiology datasets (RadImageNet, BraTS), and ask which aspects of transfer support generation. We find that: i) Natural-image initialisation consistently improves generation, by 21-34% relative gFID in pixel space against 14% in latent space, where the tokeniser supplies much of the prior. gFID gains mirror downstream pathology classification and radiomic-feature FD, both proxies for clinical fidelity. ii) Benefits reflect spatial structure, not semantics: semantic probing does not predict generation quality, whereas a spatial-structure metric adapted to internal denoiser representations tracks gFID at $|r|=0.85$, positioning spatial organisation as a channel through which pretraining manifests. iii) Mixed-domain denoiser training shows that natural and medical images share similar layer-wise representations up to the late blocks, and mixing natural images into medical training improves fidelity. iv) Transfer benefit is tied to natural image initialisation, outperforming in-domain medical pretraining and several reinitialisation schemes. Overall, natural image denoisers transfer positively to medical ones in our setup. Code is available at https://github.com/CAIROLab-Bern/rad-dit

title: From FAIR to AI-FAIR Metadata-First Infrastructure for AI-Enabled Science
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and their capabilities have advanced rapidly over the past few years, leading to widespread interest and adoption in the biological and ecological sciences. However, the data infrastructure and computational resources that provide the foundation for AI workflows in ecology and biodiversity science remain fragmented. Moreover, the flow of value remains largely unidirectional: data move from collectors, through repositories and aggregators into models, and finally to research products or management actions. The derived value, such as corrected taxonomies, annotations, quality flags, and insights, rarely returns to source communities. We propose an extension of the original FAIR principles to address the needs of AI-ready infrastructure: the AI-FAIR metadata criteria, which place AI-enabled science in the context of a bidirectional Question-Data-Model triangle. This framework is designed to facilitate large-scale content-based analysis across diverse collections and ensure that the scientists generating the data benefit from the AI-enabled advances built on their data. Alongside these criteria, we introduce an agentic evaluation workflow that both rates existing datasets on the AI-FAIR and traditional FAIR criteria and provides actionable feedback where critical metadata is missing or incomplete. This modular dataset evaluation tool, paired with a domain-appropriate checklist, translates these principles into a reusable assessment of machine-learning readiness, AI-readiness for specified tasks, traceability, and ethical and CARE-aligned stewardship. Through this approach we aim to create a community-informed system to close the model data loop, so that AI also enriches data to further enable scientific discovery.

title: From Cheap Geometry to Expensive Physics: A Physics-agnostic Pretraining Framework for Neural Operators
abstract: Industrial design evaluation often relies on high-fidelity simulations of governing partial differential equations (PDEs). While accurate, these simulations are computationally expensive, making dense exploration of design spaces impractical. Operator learning has emerged as a promising surrogate for high-fidelity physical simulations, enabling fast prediction of partial differential equation (PDE) solutions. However, accuracy of neural operators is largely affected by the amount of training data, which must be generated by expensive numerical solvers. In practical industrial scenarios, there exists large collections of candidate geometries remain unsolved due to the high computation cost. These geometry-only samples contain no physical field labels and are therefore ignored in standard operator learning pipelines. In this work, we propose a general physics-agnostic pretraining framework to exploit this abundant geometric resource to improve the performance of neural operators. Specifically, we pretrain an autoencoder on a self-supervised proxy task to reconstruct geometry (e.g., via occupancy), learning an expressive latent representation without PDE supervision. Neural operators then leverage the pretrained latent embedding to learn more effectively from limited physics labels. An error decomposition analysis is provided to help understand the effectiveness of the physics-agnostic pretraining framework. Across four PDE datasets and three state-of-the-art transformer-based neural operators, our pretraining strategy consistently improves prediction accuracy. These results demonstrate that representations from physics-agnostic pretraining provide a powerful foundation for data-efficient operator learning. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/zzzwoniu/Physics-agnostic-Operator-Pretraining.git

title: From Basis to Basis: Gaussian Particle Representation for Interpretable PDE Operators
abstract: Learning fluid PDE dynamics has increasingly benefited from neural operators and Transformer-based models, but their latent states often remain opaque, and sample-wise attention can be costly at high resolutions. We propose the \emph{Gaussian Particle Operator} (GPO), a basis-to-basis neural operator that represents fields with a learned \emph{Gaussian basis}. Each atom carries explicit geometric parameters, including centers, anisotropic scales, and weights, yielding a compact, mesh-agnostic, and directly visualizable intermediate representation. GPO operates in modal space: learned Gaussian modal windows perform Petrov--Galerkin measurements, and a PG Gaussian Attention module couples the resulting modes globally before scattering them back to the spatial domain. This design is resolution-agnostic, scales near-linearly with the number of samples for a fixed modal budget, and naturally applies to irregular geometries and 3D domains. We separately evaluate Gaussian-basis reconstruction and operator prediction. Across standard PDE benchmarks and real reanalysis datasets, GPO achieves competitive accuracy against neural-operator and Transformer baselines, ranking best on most tasks and close to the best on the remainder. The learned particles and modal couplings further provide representation-level interpretability, positioning GPO as a useful intermediate representation rather than a one-to-one decomposition of physical structures. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/lizhihao2022/GPO}.

title: From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts: Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence
abstract: For a decade, progress in artificial intelligence has been measured by how much a machine can do on its own. Large foundation models now write code and run multistep tasks, and personal agents act on a person's behalf. Yet people still forget what they once knew, miss what they are not looking at, fail to find the right words, and face hard choices without the benefit of their own history, because the machine that could help stands outside the situation. As AI moves into the physical world, attention has settled on one kind of intelligent individual, the embodied robot; we argue that the era of Physical AI holds a second kind of equal importance, the person augmented by AI. Alongside artificial general intelligence, which asks how intelligent a machine can be, stands AI-augmented human intelligence (AHI), which asks how much intelligence a machine can enable in a particular person. Realizing it calls for a new kind of system, a cognitive symbiont: a lifelong, embedded, real-time, private, low-friction, and proactive companion that senses what the person senses through external devices, keeps their context across years, models their situation and their mind, takes part in their thinking at the right moment, carries out everyday tasks with their context, and keeps learning the person as both change. We give the paradigm a conceptual core, the cognitive gap between what a person could bring to a situation and what they can hold in working memory, and organize its design space as a symbiosis loop of sensing, keeping, understanding, living alongside, acting for and thinking with the person, and growing, enclosed by a personal runtime and by trust. Because a symbiont changes what a person can do in front of others, it also raises risks of a new kind, from covert assistance in examinations to pressure on everyone to adopt it, and we treat their governance as part of the paradigm.

title: Fracture-Bench: A Controlled Benchmark Suite for Machine Learning Surrogates in Phase-Field Fracture Mechanics
abstract: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly proposed to replace phase-field fracture simulations in many-query tasks such as uncertainty quantification, inverse analysis and design. Little controlled evidence shows which architectures are reliable, for which fracture problems and how far beyond their training data. We introduce Fracture-Bench, an open benchmark of two phase-field datasets with fixed splits, common test metrics and a description of each dataset's physical regime. Dataset~1 contains 1,000 AT2 simulations of multiple cracks growing from a notched hole in a hyperelastic plate under random non-uniform biaxial boundary displacements (44 load steps, $128\times128$ grid). Dataset~2 contains 4,000 PF-CZM simulations of a pre-cracked plate with two inclusions, each ten times stiffer or more compliant than the matrix ($128\times256$ grid). We train a Fourier neural operator (FNO), DeepONet, Latent DeepONet, a UNet and a conditional diffusion model on identical splits and compare one test metric per dataset, training time, inference time and model size. On Dataset~1, FNO and Latent DeepONet attain mean test errors of order $10^{-6}$, about ten times lower than UNet and DeepONet. On Dataset~2, the diffusion model is most accurate, with about one sixth of the UNet error, but requires \SI{706}{s} per prediction versus \SI{6}{ms} for UNet. For all architectures, most of the error occurs in the final load steps, after crack localization. Dataset~2 contains initial cracks less than one grid cell apart that produce qualitatively different paths. Architecture rankings therefore depend on the task, and errors averaged over densely sampled inputs reveal little about near-bifurcation cases. Data, codes, splits, regime descriptors and generalization splits are public, with a protocol for adding under-represented regimes such as mixed-mode, three-dimensional and experimentally paired fracture.

title: Fractional is Better: Learnable Derivative Orders in Neural Operator Learning
abstract: Neural operators learn mappings between function spaces, enabling fast surrogate solutions to partial differential equations. Despite remarkable architectural diversity, these methods often share a common input representation: raw coordinate-value pairs $(x, u(x))$. We ask whether inputs aligned with PDE differential structure can improve learning. Through Picard iteration on mild solutions, we show that derivatives of the input appear explicitly in the solution operator, suggesting that providing derivative features should reduce the network's implicit differentiation burden. We prove this intuition: providing derivative features improves approximation bounds from $O(W^{-(s-m)/d})$ to $O(W^{-s/d})$, where $W$ is parameter count, $s$ is input regularity, $m$ is the PDE order, and $d$ is spatial dimension. Our central finding, however, is a surprise: the optimal derivative order $\beta^*$ is strictly less than the PDE order $m$. This gap arises from a bias-variance tradeoff in spectral space that we characterize in closed form. Learning $\beta$ from data achieves automatic spectral regularization. We introduce $\partial$-NO (del-NO), for derivative-augmented neural operators, an architecture-agnostic augmentation that provides learnable fractional derivative features to any neural operator backbone. Across benchmark problems and architectures, $\partial$-NO consistently improves prediction accuracy, with learned orders that reflect a representation of known physics modulated by noise and finite-sample constraints.
summary: Neural operators learn mappings between function spaces, enabling fast surrogate solutions to partial differential equations. Despite remarkable architectural diversity, these methods often share a common input representation: raw coordinate-value pairs $(x, u(x))$. title: Fractal basin geometry and the limits to predictability and reproducibility in deep learning
abstract: Abstract Fundamental limits to predictability are central to our understanding of many physical and computational systems. In deep learning, training outcomes are often difficult to predict and reproduce even when extrinsic sources of randomness are controlled, yet the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Here we propose riddled basin geometry as a unifying dynamical systems mechanism: every initialization leading to one solution lies arbitrarily close to initializations leading to different solutions, forming a fat fractal with structure at arbitrarily fine scales. Using a minimal neural network model, we analytically establish the classical route to riddling and derive a near-zero uncertainty exponent: even sharp increases in initialization precision yield only marginal gains in outcome predictability. In deep networks, intertwined training destinations and near-zero parameter-space exponents provide robust signatures consistent with riddling across the tested architectures, optimizers and training protocols, offering a common dynamical account of otherwise disparate empirical observations. We further introduce functional uncertainty exponents, extending these diagnostics of scale-insensitive irreproducibility from parameter space to the learned functions themselves. Together, our results support riddled basin geometry as a candidate organizing principle for irreproducibility in deep learning, with practical implications for optimization and the reliable deployment of artificial intelligence.

title: Foundation model for particle collision data analysis
abstract: Abstract Data-intensive collider experiments increasingly require models that transfer across high-dimensional, partially observed measurements, yet most analyses still optimize separate models for each task. Here, to address this bottleneck, we introduce EVENET, an event-level foundation model pretrained on 500 million simulated collision events using self-supervised learning and physics-informed supervision. The model constructs a shared particle-cloud representation from the variable-length set of physics objects in each event. Across searches for heavy resonances and exotic Higgs decays, EVENET outperforms both established and state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in low-statistics regimes. We validate transfer to experimental data by rediscovering the ϒ meson in CMS Open Data. The pretrained model also supports precise extraction of quantum-correlation observables that remain stable under the tested systematic variations. Together, these results establish a reusable backbone for diverse collider analyses, improving downstream adaptation after a substantial one-time pretraining investment.

title: Forward and inverse resolvent modelling for instabilities and active control in compressible boundary layers using a Transformer neural operator
abstract: Resolvent analysis effectively characterises flow instabilities and guides active control, but repeated singular-value-decomposition-based (SVD-based) calculations remain computationally expensive in high-dimensional parameter studies. Control-oriented workflows also require efficient mappings from prescribed response fields to compatible forcing fields. To address these needs, we introduce ResFormer, a unified Transformer-based neural operator framework for forward resolvent prediction and response-to-forcing reconstruction in compressible boundary layers. The framework is validated across supersonic and hypersonic regimes ( italic Ma equals 2.25 Ma = 2.25 $ \textit{Ma}=2.25$ – 5.86 5.86 $5.86$ ), encompassing laminar, turbulent and controlled base-flow configurations. For forward prediction, ResFormer reconstructs the spatial topology, phase structure and amplitude envelope of both low-frequency Tollmien–Schlichting waves and high-frequency second-mode disturbances over the investigated parameter ranges. For response-to-forcing prediction, ResFormer learns a surrogate mapping from prescribed instability responses to compatible forcing fields. When the complete target response and discrete operator are known, the reference forcing is computed directly as ModifyingAbove bold italic f With caret Subscript italic ideal Baseline equals bold italic upper A Subscript omega comma beta Baseline ModifyingAbove bold italic q With caret Subscript italic decay f ^ ideal = A ω , β q ^ decay $\kern2.5pt \hat {\boldsymbol{\kern-2.5pt f}}_{\textit{ideal}}=\boldsymbol{A}_{\omega ,\beta }\hat {\boldsymbol{q}}_{\textit{decay}}$ ; the physics term therefore acts as an operator consistency regulariser. The reconstructed forcing topology is then reduced to a compact Gaussian wall actuator prior and evaluated using high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics. ResFormer therefore accelerates repeated SVD-based forward and optimal mode evaluations while providing an operator-consistent learned representation for actuator prior identification and surrogate-assisted control design.

title: Fluid–structure interaction in a square array of submerged flexible stems
abstract: The evolution of flow structure is fundamental to establishing an accurate framework for predicting turbulent energy dissipation, momentum transfer, and sediment and nutrient transport within and above flexible stem arrays. The dynamics of flexible stems plays a crucial role in shaping these physical features. In this paper, direct numerical simulations are performed to examine flow through a three-dimensional square array of flexible stems, with explicit consideration of flexibility ( upper K K $K$ ) effects. The results provide a comprehensive characterisation of the coupled stem dynamics, flow distribution and vortex structures. Three distinct dynamical regimes are identified. For large upper K K $K$ , the stems behave as nearly rigid, causing the flow to accelerate through the gaps while attenuating behind the stems. At intermediate upper K K $K$ , a perfect lock-in occurs between the stem’s natural and oscillation frequencies, leading to large-amplitude vibrations and markedly altered flow characteristics. For small upper K K $K$ , the oscillation amplitude decreases but deformation increases, producing irregular stem dynamics and complex flow features. The flow dynamics underlying these regimes is systematically elucidated. Furthermore, energy dissipation and sediment transport effects are quantified through hydrodynamic drag, bed shear stress, and root mean square bed shear friction distributions. The array with intermediate upper K K $K$ exhibits the highest energy dissipation efficiency, surpassing even the rigid configuration. The bed shear stress reaches a peak at the upstream edge of the array, whereas stem oscillation redistributes the flow momentum towards the upper canopy and the overlying flow, reducing velocity fluctuations near the bed. Finally, the mechanisms governing the structural dynamics and hydrodynamic forces are discussed in detail. This study offers new physical insights into flow–structure interactions within flexible stem arrays, and proposes an optimised strategy for improving energy dissipation in coastal protection applications.

title: Fluid structure interaction in wind-sensitive structures: Flow mechanisms, coupled modeling, and reduced-order prediction
abstract: Fluid–structure interaction (FSI) in wind-sensitive structures arises from a closed exchange among separated flow, surface traction, structural motion, and wake reorganization. This review compares experiments, numerical methods, reduced-order models, and learned surrogates through the feedback and interface quantities they retain. Mono-directional analysis is distinguished from bi-directional FSI according to whether the computed structural motion is returned to the flow. That distinction determines which pressure phase, wake state, and aerodynamic work can be represented. The synthesis leads to two conclusions. First, agreement in force or response amplitude alone is insufficient near an instability boundary because an error in load–motion phase can reverse the inferred aerodynamic work. Second, neither fine flow field resolution nor a learning architecture guarantees power-consistent transfer across a moving interface; this property must be imposed or verified separately. Experimental methods are therefore assessed through synchronized load, motion, and flow observables, and numerical and learned models through interface consistency, response regime coverage, and uncertainty. These criteria guide model selection for bluff-body vibration, bridge and building response, flexible membranes, and related wind-sensitive systems.

title: FlowPET: Physics-Informed Symplectic Flow Matching for Low-Count PET Reconstruction
abstract: Low-count Positron Emission Tomography (PET) reconstruction is severely hindered by the dissipative nature of prevailing generative models, where the inherent phase-space contraction leads to the numerical extinction (``wash-out'') of weak but diagnostically critical lesion signals. To overcome this geometric limitation, we propose \textbf{FlowPET}, a physics-informed framework that reformulates reconstruction as volume-preserving transport in a symplectic phase space. By parameterizing the posterior dynamics via a Separable Hamiltonian System, our approach guarantees a divergence-free vector field by construction, theoretically immunizing weak signals against probability mass collapse. To steer this conservative flow, we introduce conjugate boundary conditions based on the Range-Null space decomposition of the PET operator; this strictly enforces data consistency in the range space while confining stochastic uncertainty injection to the unobserved null space. We train the model via symplectic flow matching and perform inference using a symplectic leapfrog integrator. Extensive experiments on BrainWeb, clinical pediatric, and UDPET datasets demonstrate that \textbf{FlowPET} not only surpasses state-of-the-art deterministic and stochastic baselines in SSIM and PSNR but, more crucially, exhibits superior recovery of low-contrast lesions. The results confirm that imposing Hamiltonian structural constraints offers a robust geometric safeguard for medical inverse problems in high-noise regimes.

title: Flow-Guided Neural Operator For Self- Supervised Learning On Time Series Data
abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) is a powerful paradigm for learning from unlabeled time-series data. However, popular methods such as masked autoencoders (MAEs) rely on reconstructing inputs from a fixed, predetermined masking ratio. Instead of this static design, we propose treating the corruption level as a new degree of freedom for representation learning, enhancing flexibility and performance. To achieve this, we introduce the Flow-Guided Neural Operator (FGNO), a novel framework combining operator learning with flow matching for SSL training. By leveraging Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) to enable computation under different time resolutions, our approach effectively learns mappings in functional spaces. We extract a rich hierarchy of features by tapping into different network layers ($l$) and flow times ($s$) that apply varying strengths of noise to the input data. This enables the extraction of versatile representations, from low-level patterns to high-level semantics, using a single model adaptable to specific tasks. Unlike prior generative SSL methods that use noisy inputs during inference, we propose using clean inputs for representation extraction while learning representations with noise; this eliminates randomness and boosts accuracy. We evaluate FGNO across three biomedical domains, where it consistently outperforms established baselines. Our method yields up to 35\% AUROC gains in neural signal decoding (BrainTreeBank), 16\% RMSE reductions in skin temperature prediction (DREAMT), and over 20\% improvement in accuracy and macro-F1 on SleepEDF under low-data regimes. These results highlight FGNO’s robustness to data scarcity and its superior capacity to learn expressive representations for diverse time-series applications.

title: Flow mechanisms of flying fish during free-surface taxiing
abstract: This study numerically investigates the flow mechanisms of a four-winged flying fish during free-surface taxiing, the pivotal phase enabling long-distance aerial gliding. Under identical kinematic parameters, the caudal fin yields substantial thrust (C¯T,tail≈1.22) during free-surface taxiing, in contrast to the negative value obtained in deep-water swimming (C¯T,tail≈−3.79), indicating that the free surface fundamentally alters the thrust-generation mechanism. Wake analyses reveal that the undulating caudal fin generates periodic depression waves, which reshape the vortex structure and drive the formation of a unique staggered 2S* vortex mode in the water phase; within this mode, each vortex independently induces intense streamwise momentum jets, thereby contributing to thrust generation. In addition, free-surface taxiing exhibits a markedly higher lift (CL≈2.15) compared to aerial gliding (CL≈0.57). Lift distribution undergoes a significant shift: the pectoral fins provide 85% of the total lift during aerial gliding, whereas the caudal fin contributes over 60% during taxiing, replacing the pectoral fins as the primary lift generator. This dominance stems from the substantial pressure differential induced by the density contrast between the media. Further parametric analysis demonstrates that efficient propulsion requires a pronounced 2S* vortex mode. Low-amplitude undulation produces shallow and narrow depression waves that fail to form the 2S* mode, resulting in ineffective propulsion. Meanwhile, excessively high frequency or wavelength causes depression waves to merge, disrupting the 2S* vortex street and substantially reducing propulsive efficiency. The optimal parameters are identified as A*≈0.2, St ≈0.85 , and λ*≈1. These results clarify how free-surface deformation couples with caudal-fin undulation to enhance propulsion and lift.

title: Flow in a narrow-gap annulus: drag reduction by inner cylinder azimuthal oscillation
abstract: The axial flow through a thin gap between two concentric cylinders is investigated using direct numerical simulation (DNS) of the Navier–Stokes equations. It is shown that by imposing a stationary, harmonic, azimuthal velocity at the inner cylinder wall, drag reduction is always attained while power saving is limited to a portion of the explored amplitude–axial wavelength space. The largest values of drag reduction and power saving are 44 percent sign 44 % $44\,\%$ and 11 percent sign 11 % $11\,\%$ , respectively, obtained for different amplitude–axial wavelength pairs. It has been verified that the effect of such a control on a convex surface aligns well with the known concept in plane channel flows of depressing in turn the pressure–strain, the radial Reynolds stress, the turbulent shear stress and ultimately the viscous drag. A direct connection between the wall motion, through the Stokes layer, and the pressure–strain reduction has been identified as the root cause of the passive flow control effectiveness.
