title: Decouple to Reuse: Fine-Grained Knowledge Augmentation for Time Series Foundation Models
abstract: Time series forecasting is critical for demand prediction and resource management in modern Web services, yet applying pretrained Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) to downstream tasks remains challenging due to domain shifts. Existing retrieval-augmented approaches typically retrieve coarse-grained window contexts and may introduce context-specific noise. To address this problem, we argue that temporal patterns should be reused at a decomposition level, as effective trend and seasonal dynamics may originate from different contexts. We propose \method, a two-stage \underline{F}ine-grained \underline{K}nowledge \underline{A}ugmentation framework that decouples and consolidates pre-training knowledge into compact, task-shared residual codebooks to enhance frozen TSFMs. Specifically, Stage I constructs dual-branch residual codebooks for decoupled trend and seasonal signals, while Stage II dynamically retrieves and merges these fine-grained patterns into target representations via task-adaptive aggregation and gate fusion. Extensive experiments across eight real-world benchmarks with four representative TSFM backbones demonstrate the superior effectiveness and computational efficiency of \method, while further validating the strong transferability of the residual codebooks across different backbones. The source code is available at the anonymous repository: https://github.com/yuppielqx/TSFM-Component-Token-Adapter

title: Decompose, Structure, and Repair: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Autoformalization via Operator Trees
abstract: Statement autoformalization acts as a critical bridge between human mathematics and formal mathematics by translating natural language problems into formal language. While prior works have focused on data synthesis and diverse training paradigms to optimize end-to-end Large Language Models (LLMs), they typically treat formal code as flat sequences, neglecting the hierarchical logic inherent in mathematical statements. In this work, we introduce Decompose, Structure, and Repair (DSR), a neuro-symbolic framework that restructures autoformalization into a modular pipeline. DSR decomposes statements into logical components and maps them to structured operator trees, leveraging this topological blueprint to precisely localize and repair errors via sub-tree refinement. Furthermore, we introduce PRIME, a benchmark of 156 undergraduate and graduate-level theorems selected from canonical textbooks and expertly annotated in Lean 4. Experimental results demonstrate that DSR establishes a new state-of-the-art, consistently outperforming baselines under equivalent computational budgets. The datasets, model, and code are available at https://github.com/XiaoyangLiu-sjtu/DSR.

title: Decompose the Distillation: Interpretable Single-Pass Guidance for Diffusion Models
abstract: Classifier-Free Guidance is a widely used inference-time guidance rule for conditional image generation with diffusion models, which exposes a guidance scale that adjusts conditioning strength after training. This flexibility requires conditional and unconditional model evaluations at every sampling step, so an N-step trajectory takes 2N forward passes. Single-pass alternatives reduce such cost, yet most collapse CFG's two components into one opaque guided prediction, losing the separable base flow and guidance direction that support per-step control and diagnostics, even when the scale remains adjustable. This work introduces CtrlFlow, a single-pass guidance method that preserves CFG's separable base-flow and guidance-direction interface. To preserve both components at one-pass cost, CtrlFlow attaches two lightweight LoRA adapters to a frozen backbone, each adding 2.5% parameters, and predicts the base flow and guidance direction from one pass of the shared frozen backbone. Because the guidance scale multiplies the guidance direction only after the forward pass, one evaluation yields the guided velocity at any scale, so a single trained checkpoint remains adjustable at inference without retraining. Preserving two outputs introduces a training mismatch: inference amplifies guidance-direction errors by the chosen scale, while naive component-wise losses weight both outputs equally. To align training with this composed inference-time error, CtrlFlow uses a unified multi-scale distillation loss. Residual guidance errors can still persist at extreme scales, where even small guidance-direction errors are amplified by the guidance scale. To reduce this inference-time error, CtrlFlow applies scale-adaptive modulation to damp velocity-field errors and time-grid warping to concentrate solver evaluations where the trajectory changes most rapidly.

title: Decoder Only Transformer for Physics Informed Neural Networks
abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) approximate PDE solutions by embedding physical constraints into training, yet MLP-based backbones often suffer from instability and loss of fidelity on long horizons. Recent sequence models (e.g., Transformers) alleviate some of these issues, but their encoder–decoder design adds parameters and memory pressure with limited benefit for autoregressive pseudo-sequences. We introduce \textbf{DoPformer}, a \emph{decoder-only} Transformer tailored to physics-informed learning. DoPformer consumes short spatio–temporal pseudo-sequences, uses multi-head self-attention with WaveAct activations, and applies a sequential physics loss across the window. Removing the encoder and cross-attention yields a lighter model while preserving long-range temporal coupling through self-attention. To further boost spectral accuracy, we explore two optional modules: (i) a Fourier \emph{neural-operator} branch (\textit{DoPformer+NO}) that improves oscillatory regimes and long-horizon rollouts; and (ii) a compact \emph{KAN}-based feed-forward replacement (\textit{DoPformer+KAN}) that drastically reduces parameters while maintaining strong accuracy. Across convection, reaction, wave, and 2D Navier–Stokes equations, DoPformer consistently improves PINN accuracy and stability; the NO and KAN variants deliver additional gains depending on stiffness and spectral content. Our numerical results show that on these benchmarks DoPformer attains state-of-the-art accuracy among physics-informed models while using substantially fewer parameters.

title: Deciding two-variable logic with global and local Presburger quantification
abstract: We look at a two-variable logic over finite graphs that allows Presburger quantifiers: linear arithmetic inequalities between the number of elements that satisfy subformulas. The prior literature shows that closing two-variable logic under Presburger quantification leads to undecidability, while closing under \emph{local quantification} -- the counts are always over neighbors of a given node -- preserves decidability. Here we show decidability of satisfiability for an intermediate logic that allows both local counts and global counts, but where the linear constraints do not mix the two. The proof requires a significant extension of the prior machinery developed for two-variable logic with counting. As a corollary we obtain decidability of satisfiability for an important family of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). GNNs are a popular graph learning formalism. For example, in a variation of GNNs considered in the past literature, local aggregation is used in each layer to create modified values at each vertex of a graph, and then global aggregation is used in a final layer to obtain a single numerical value for the graph as a whole. Our logic is motivated by the fact that mixing of local counting and global aggregation in GNNs has been shown to lead to undecidability. Our results here show that if global and local aggregation are separated, one regains decidability. Decidability of other static analysis problems, like equivalence of GNNs, follows from the decidability of satisfiability.

title: DecAEvolve: Decompose, Adapt, and Evolve, or Three Pillars of Effective LLM-based Scientific Equation Discovery
abstract: Finding mathematical relations underlying natural phenomena and scientific systems has been one of the fundamental tasks in the history of scientific discovery. Recent advancements in evolutionary search with Large Language Models (LLMs), with their embedded scientific knowledge, have shown great promise for this task. However, discovering such mathematical models governing scientific observations still remains significantly challenging, as it requires navigating vast combinatorial hypothesis spaces with an explosion of possible relations. Existing LLM-based approaches overlook the impact of data on the structure of mathematical relations, and treat LLMs as a static hypothesis generator unaware of the observed scientific system. This leads to suboptimal and inefficient exploration of the hypothesis space with over-reliance on LLMs' internal priors. To bridge this gap, we introduce Decompose, Adapt, and Evolve (DecAEvolve), a framework that leverages granular feedback from symbolic term decomposition and LLM refinement through reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning to enhance both robustness and efficiency of evolutionary discovery frameworks. Our experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate that DecAEvolve significantly improves the accuracy of discovered equations and the efficiency of the discovery process compared to the state-of-the-art baselines.

title: DecAEvolve: Decompose, Adapt, and Evolve for Effective LLM-based Scientific Equation Discovery
abstract: Finding mathematical relations underlying natural phenomena is a fundamental task in scientific discovery. Recent advances in evolutionary search with Large Language Models (LLMs) show great promise by leveraging their embedded scientific knowledge. However, discovering governing equations remains challenging due to vast combinatorial hypothesis spaces with exponentially many possible relations. Existing LLM-based approaches treat LLMs as static hypothesis generators unaware of the observed scientific system, leading to suboptimal and inefficient exploration that over-relies on internal priors. To address this, we introduce Decompose, Adapt, and Evolve (DecAEvolve), a framework that combines granular feedback from symbolic term decomposition with LLM refinement through reinforcement learning fine-tuning. DecAEvolve unifies symbolic decomposition with test-time RL adaptation, enabling adaptive rather than static hypothesis generation. Our experiments across diverse scientific benchmarks demonstrate that DecAEvolve significantly improves both the accuracy of discovered equations and the efficiency of the discovery process, reducing error by up to an order of magnitude compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

title: De Rham cohomological architectures for PINNs and PDEs with topological holes
abstract: We attempt to alleviate failure modes of classical physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in scenarios of topological pathologies corresponding to punctures, holes, poles, and voids by introducing de Rham cohomological augmentations, or Hodge-de Rham PINNs. Vanilla PINNs often encounter pitfalls in hole-based settings due to discontinuous interfaces, nonzero closed path integration, path dependence, correspondence to exact forms via the exterior derivative, etc., therefore we absolve traditional failures via parameterizing a 1-form by the Hodge-Morrey-Friedrichs (HMF) decomposition for manifolds with boundary, drawing a connection to de Rham cohomology such as through the HMF isomorphism theorem. 1-forms can act as representations of scalar-valued PDE solutions through integral operator mappings. We propose performing a PINN-based loss on the parameterized 1-form through an associated PDE, which subsequently solves the potential-based PINN problem and moreover remedies the failures of vanilla PINNs via the Sobolev-regular operator under a Fréchet differentiation interconnection. The operator relationship often has a nontrivial closed-form and often requires integration or a case-by-case analysis, which we address thoroughly in our experiments. When an integrability condition is not met on our losses, we can equip exhaustion functions to train the networks. We demonstrate our methods on the Aharonov-Bohm effect, which, to our understanding, is largely nonexistent in PINN literature. We develop theoretical guarantees of our methods and demonstrate our pathological safeguards on a broad selection of topologically-adverse problems, including scenarios of inexact forms, and those of nontrivial harmonics and coexact terms.

title: D$^2$O: A Dual Debiasing Operator for Training-Free Test-Time Adaptation of Vision–Language Models
abstract: Training-free test-time adaptation (TTA) for vision-language models (VLMs) can improve zero-shot classification under mild shifts, but often degrades under severe style/environment variation. We identify two shared failure modes in training-free pipelines: (i) retrieval confounding, where feature similarity is dominated by nuisance/style variation and corrupts retrieval evidence; and (ii) environment-biased priors, where VLM logits exhibit environment-dependent centered shifts that distort gating and prior-like terms. Therefore, we propose D$^2$O, a training-free debiasing operator that outputs three inference-time objects: a retrieval-oriented content feature for semantic matching, a style-aware routing coordinate for bias tracking, and debiased logits for corrected priors. D$^2$O composes plug-and-play with retrieval-based and closed-form Gaussian adapters in online and transductive settings. We further provide operator-to-decision guarantees: finite-difference covariance recovers a nuisance-sensitive subspace, routing-based EMA controls centered-logit template estimates, and these errors yield bounded pairwise score perturbations, leading to a margin-based condition for label invariance. Extensive experiments show that D$^2$O achieves its clearest gains under style/environment-dominant shifts, with broader gains elsewhere. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/MAiTL-Group/D2O}.

title: Coupled transport and adsorption in graded filters: A multi-scale analysis of non-solenoidal effects
abstract: We investigate the transport and adsorption of solutes within graded porous filters characterised by a spatially varying microstructure. While classical homogenisation theory typically assumes periodic media, we employ the method of multiple scales to derive an effective macroscopic model for ‘near-periodic’ geometries where the porosity varies slowly over the longitudinal coordinate. A key novelty of this work is the departure from the standard solenoidal constraint; instead, we introduce a modified incompressibility condition derived from non-equilibrium thermodynamics that accounts for the coupling between the solute concentration and the solvent velocity. This leads to a generalised Darcy-scale description where the fluid velocity field is non-solenoidal within the porous domain. Through asymptotic analysis, we determine the leading-order concentration profiles and quantify first-order corrections that capture the interplay between the porosity gradient and the mixture composition. We evaluate filter performance across several metrics, including outflux concentration and total adsorption rate, under both fixed-flow and fixed-pressure-drop operating conditions. Our results demonstrate that the porosity gradient and the coupling parameter significantly influence the filtration efficiency, particularly as the medium approaches the clogging limit. The analysis reveals that the optimal filter design is highly sensitive to the chosen performance metric, highlighting the necessity of physically consistent boundary conditions and mixture dynamics in the design of high-efficiency graded filters.

title: CounterFactual Retrieval for Evidence-Aware Individual Animal Identification
abstract: Automated identification of individual animals is moving from small curated studies toward shared benchmarks and reusable foundation models. This progress is useful, but current evaluation leaves the evidence behind a match unresolved, i.e., high retrieval accuracy does not show whether a model used animal features or identity-correlated shortcuts. We address this with Counterfactual Foreground Retrieval (CFR), an evidence-aware evaluation protocol. CFR evaluates the same query-gallery task under different views: full image, foreground-only, and shortcut-only. The full-image measures standard retrieval performance; the foreground-only measures foreground-supported retrieval; and shortcut-only view measure how much identity signal is recoverable from background, or silhouette. This turns a retrieval score into an evidence profile: how well the model performs on the original images, how much of that performance remains when only the animal is visible, and how much identity signal remains recoverable when the animal is removed. We release around 0.5M masks for 34 datasets and code for mask generation and CFR evaluation.

title: Convex Distance Operator Transport: A Convex and Geometry-Preserving Formulation
abstract: We introduce Convex Distance Operator Transport (CDOT), the first convex optimal transport framework that aligns distributions across heterogeneous domains by jointly preserving feature correspondence and intrinsic geometric structure. Specifically, CDOT employs an operator-based regularization that aligns aggregated distance structures by introducing distance and conditional expectation operators. Consequently, the proposed regularization improves the robustness to local geometric variations. We further prove that the resulting CDOT discrepancy is a valid pseudometric on the space of attributed compact metric-measure spaces. In addition, we characterize the relationship between CDOT and Gromov--Wasserstien (GW) through a new notion of dispersion gap, formally elucidating the geometric source of non-convexity in GW compared to the convexity of CDOT. In the finite-sample regime, we derive a non-asymptotic risk bound decomposed into optimization and statistical errors, establishing risk consistency under a globally convergent Frank--Wolfe algorithm. Experiments on synthetic point clouds, brain connectomes, and graph classification benchmarks demonstrate better performance over existing methods, with stable and reliable behavior in practice.

title: Control Foundation Models across Changing Block Diagrams: Generalizing Time-Series Prediction to Dynamic Graphs
abstract: In the prediction and control of physical systems, combining records from different experiments and operations is expected to supply information that no single experiment provides on its own. Time-series foundation models, which learn a shared predictor from diverse time series, offer a framework for treating such records as a common training resource. Moreover, query-based prediction models, which switch between known and target signals within the same time series, make it possible to handle response prediction and control-input generation in a unified manner. However, in control-experiment data, the connections between signals change with the experimental stage, such as system identification, filtering, and feedback control, which calls for a formulation that handles signal values and connection structures dynamically and in a unified way. We formulate a control foundation model that defines a data space of dynamic graphs containing connections, signal values, and missing values, together with an operation on this space that specifies the known signals and the prediction targets. This allows response prediction and control-input generation to be described as a common masked prediction problem, even for experimental data with different connections and recorded signals. The Block Diagram Transformer (BDT), which implements this formulation, combines attention along the time axis with a graph neural network that follows the block-diagram connections, and can be initialized with the pretrained parameters of existing time-series foundation models. Trained on control-experiment data that mix multiple experimental settings, the proposed model stabilized an unstable system through feedback control, which is difficult to achieve by fine-tuning existing time-series foundation models. Ongoing work applying this approach to a wide range of target systems is also yielding promising results.

title: Contrasting epigenetic dynamics in chromosome arms and pericentromeres during ROS1-induced plant immune memory
abstract: Abstract Immune memory enables plants to respond more effectively to recurrent pathogen infections. Epigenetic changes in DNA methylation and small RNAs have been implicated, yet how their temporal dynamics govern immune memory establishment and erasure remains unclear. Using a chemically inducible system to activate the DNA demethylase REPRESSOR OF SILENCING 1 (ROS1) in Arabidopsis, we establish immune memory against biotrophic pathogens that persists for at least one week. Memory establishment coincides with reduced small RNA accumulation and DNA methylation along chromosome arms, including at promoters of genes involved in salicylic acid–dependent immunity and DNA damage repair. These changes are progressively reversed during immune memory erasure. In contrast, transposon-rich pericentromeres retain elevated small RNA and DNA methylation levels, consistent with a CLASSY3-associated redistribution of RNA-directed DNA methylation. Our findings show that transient ROS1 activity drives contrasting epigenetic responses across chromosomal regions, shaping both the establishment and erasure of plant immune memory.

title: Context parroting: A simple but tough-to-beat baseline for foundation models in scientific machine learning
abstract: Recent time-series foundation models exhibit strong abilities to predict physical systems. These abilities include zero-shot forecasting, in which a model forecasts future states of a system given only a short trajectory as context, without knowledge of the underlying physics. Here, we show that foundation models often forecast through a simple parroting strategy, and when they are not parroting they exhibit some shared failure modes such as converging to the mean. As a result, a naive context parroting model that copies directly from the context scores higher than leading time-series foundation models on predicting a diverse range of dynamical systems, including low-dimensional chaos, turbulence, coupled oscillators, and electrocardiograms, at a tiny fraction of the computational cost. We draw a parallel between context parroting and induction heads, which explains recent works showing that large language models can often be repurposed for time series forecasting. Our dynamical systems perspective also ties the scaling between forecast accuracy and context length to the fractal dimension of the underlying chaotic attractor, providing insight into previously observed in-context neural scaling laws. By revealing the performance gaps and failure modes of current time-series foundation models, context parroting can guide the design of future foundation models and help identify in-context learning strategies beyond parroting.

title: Computations on locomotion of spheroidal particle driven by force and torque in shear-thinning fluid
abstract: Shear-thinning is a typical non-Newtonian rheological characteristic of biological fluids such as blood and mucus. Extensive studies have been conducted on self-propelled particles. The dynamics of externally actuated particles in non-Newtonian fluids have garnered widespread attention in recent years. Understanding the dynamic behavior of externally driven micro-particles in complex media is crucial for their biomedical applications. In this work, we employ the finite element method to numerically simulate the motion characteristics of spheroidal particles in shear-thinning fluids under two actuation modes: force-induced translation and torque-driven rotation, by coupling the continuity equation, momentum conservation equation, and the Carreau constitutive equation. The results show that particle eccentricity e affects the non-uniform distribution of local apparent viscosity, which is an important factor influencing the particle's locomotion speed. Furthermore, by quantifying the effects of the viscosity ratio β and Carreau number Cu on particle motion characteristics under the two modes, it is revealed that the non-uniform distribution of local shear rate induced by particle geometric anisotropy is the core mechanism governing the motion performance. These results provide useful guidance for the design of externally driven microrobots operating in biological media.

title: Complex-ray extraction of flat-plate leading-edge receptivity with finite-distance corrections
abstract: Leading-edge receptivity converts free-stream forcing into downstream Tollmien–Schlichting waves through the first Lam–Rott mode. We develop a direct asymptotic formulation to control finite-distance bias in the extracted receptivity coefficient. A further Fredholm condition and main-deck matching determine distinct corrections for displacement and wall-shear estimators under common scaling, phase, and normalization conventions. These correction coefficients are evaluated before comparison with computed ray solutions. Seven rays spanning both halves of the dominance sector test the resulting extraction over four common windows. The correction reduces maximum pairwise distances between complex coefficients by factors of 24–60. The maximum corrected displacement–shear difference is approximately 1.67×10−4, while normal-grid and marching changes remain below the predeclared 2.5×10−4 tolerance. The measured remainder decay is consistent with the predicted O(χ−2) order over the tested range. Together, the explicit correction and resolution checks provide reproducible finite-window controls for complex-amplitude extraction in the stated flat-plate problem.

title: Comparative analysis of end-to-end learning and foundation models for clinical-grade prostate pathology
abstract: Abstract Foundation models (FMs) using self-supervised pre-training are widely advocated as a universal solution for pathology, yet their advantages over task-specific (TS) models remain unclear. Here we show, using over 100,000 prostate biopsies from 6268 patients across 15 sites, that while FMs demonstrate utility in data-scarce scenarios, their performance converges with—and is in some cases surpassed by—TS models with sufficient labeled training data. Concordance with pathologists’ grading reaches quadratic Cohen’s kappas of 0.91 (95% CI 0.90-0.92; all models) on internal and 0.87 (0.86-0.88; TS), 0.86 (0.84-0.87; UNI FM) and 0.85 (0.84-0.86; Virchow2 FM) on external cohorts at full training. Task-specific training markedly reduces misgrading, misdiagnosis of challenging morphologies, and technical variability. Notably, FMs consume up to 35 times more energy. We advocate for considering both FMs and end-to-end learning for robust, resource-efficient, and clinically applicable AI pathology.

title: CoEvol-NO: State and Coordinate Co-Evolution with an Error-Driven Predictor-Corrector Paradigm for Neural Operator Transformer
abstract: Despite the fast progress in neural operator learning, long-sequence modeling still is a standing challenge whereby latent states have been introduced with techniques well derived. Diverging from existing methods that treat latent states as transient variables or decoupled representations, CoEvol-NO introduces a persistent state to establish a co-evolutionary framework, where the latent state and mesh sequence are updated jointly and bidirectionally. Inspired by classical numerical methods, we model the layer-wise state evolution as a Predictor-Corrector (PC) process. Specifically, a "Predictor'' generates a tentative target, followed by a "Corrector'' that refines the persistent state via an {error-driven update mechanism}. Furthermore, our theoretical analysis reveals that the widely used \textit{direct substitution} and \textit{residual update} paradigms are essentially {first-order approximations} of this error-driven correction under different loss assumptions. We theoretically prove that CoEvol-NO achieves strict linear time complexity. Extensive experiments on five standard benchmarks and two large-scale industrial design tasks demonstrate that CoEvol-NO consistently achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance.

title: Cluster Attention for Graph Machine Learning
abstract: Message passing neural networks have recently become the most popular approach to graph machine learning tasks, however, their receptive field is limited by the number of message-passing layers. To increase the receptive field, using graph transformers with global attention has been proposed, however, global attention does not take into account the graph topology and thus lacks graph-structure-based inductive biases which are typically very important for graph machine learning tasks. In this work, we propose an alternative approach: cluster attention (CLATT). We divide graph nodes into clusters with off-the-shelf graph community detection algorithms and let each node attend to all other nodes in each cluster. CLATT provides large receptive fields while still having strong graph-structure-based inductive biases. We show that augmenting message-passing neural networks or graph transformers with CLATT significantly improves their performance on a wide range of graph datasets including datasets from the recently introduced GraphLand benchmark representing real-world applications of graph machine learning.

title: CloudNFMM: A Hybrid Hierarchical and Local Neural Operator Inspired by the Fast Multipole Method
abstract: The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) is an efficient numerical algorithm used to calculate long-range forces in many-body problems, leveraging hierarchical data structures and series expansions. In this work, we present the Cloud Neural FMM (CloudNFMM), a new neural operator architecture that integrates the hierarchical structure of the FMM to learn the Green's operator of elliptic PDEs on point cloud data. The architecture efficiently learns representations for both local and far-field interactions. The core innovation is the local attention, a specialised local attention mechanism which models complex dependencies within a small neighbourhood of points. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, and discuss possible extensions and modifications to the CloudNFMM architecture.

title: Clipped Q-Learning: Your Value Clipping Is Secretly A Robust Operator
abstract: We study a simple yet principled modification of classical Q-learning that clips the value estimate in the Bellman backup by a threshold $\lambda$. The resulting algorithm, clipped Q-learning, is motivated by a key theoretical insight: the clipped Bellman backup is an unbiased one-sample estimation of a robust Bellman operator arising naturally from a transition-regularized MDP framework. This formulation corresponds to optimizing performance against a specific class of adversarial dynamics perturbations at the test time that reallocate transition probability mass away from high-value states, thereby inducing conservative but stable decision making. Under this interpretation, clipped Q-learning can be viewed as tracking the fixed point of the robust Bellman equation and learning policies that hedge against adversarial dynamics shifts at test time. We analyze two clipped Q-learning variants with an optimistic exploration bonus and establish polynomial regret guarantees, demonstrating statistical efficiency. Beyond the tabular setting, our framework suggests that value clipping is a modular mechanism that can be incorporated into general value-based RL algorithms with function approximation. As a proof of concept, we evaluate a clipped Double DQN algorithm on a control task and observe robustness improvements consistent with our theoretical predictions.

title: Clade-specific transmission dynamics of enterovirus D68 and their association with acute flaccid myelitis
abstract: Abstract Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) is a common cause of mild respiratory illness in children but is also linked to acute flaccid myelitis (AFM), a rare and severe neurological condition which can result in permanent paralysis. Tracking EV-D68 transmission is difficult because symptoms overlap with other common childhood illnesses, making case reporting unreliable. As a result, the burden of EV-D68 transmission remains poorly understood, particularly prior to the first widely recognised outbreak in 2014. Phylodynamic approaches offer a powerful alternative to case-based surveillance, inferring epidemiological parameters directly from pathogen genetic sequences. Here we show, using a birth-death-sampling phylodynamic model applied to publicly available EV-D68 sequences from the 1990s to 2023 collected in Europe and North America, that seasonal EV-D68 transmission was well established long before the 2014 outbreak brought the virus to widespread attention. Furthermore, we show that AFM case burden is strongly associated with the transmission dynamics of a specific EV-D68 clade, clade B, an association not seen for clades A and D. These findings suggest that clade-specific biological differences drive AFM risk, with important implications for surveillance prioritisation and the timing of future burden of neurological disease.

title: Certifying Graph Neural Networks Against Label and Structure Poisoning
abstract: Robust machine learning for graph-structured data has made significant progress against test-time attacks, yet certified robustness to poisoning - where adversaries manipulate the training data - remains largely underexplored. For image data, state-of-the-art poisoning certificates rely on partitioning-and-aggregation schemes. However, we show that these methods fail when applied in the graph domain due to the inherent label and structure sparsity found in common graph datasets, making effective graph-partitioning difficult. To address this challenge, we propose a novel semi-supervised learning framework called deep Self-Training Graph Partition Aggregation (ST-GPA), which enriches each graph partition with informative pseudo-labels and synthetic edges, enabling effective certification against node-label and graph-structure poisoning under sparse conditions. Our method is architecture-agnostic, scales to large numbers of partitions, and consistently and significantly improves robustness guarantees against both label and structure poisoning across multiple benchmarks, while maintaining strong clean accuracy. Overall, our results establish a promising direction for certifiably robust learning on graph-structured data against poisoning under sparse conditions.

title: Cavitation in translational brain impacts: The role of cerebrospinal fluid pressure and brain deformation dynamics
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) affects an estimated 69 million people worldwide annually and is associated with neurological disability. However, injury mechanisms and outcomes remain poorly understood, limiting protective and treatment strategies. The pressure response of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) has gained attention due to evidence of intracranial cavitation. However, the severity of CSF pressurization remains unexplored. This study introduces an experimental system to examine CSF flow during translational impacts on the head by analyzing brain strain distribution, CSF pressurization, and skull acceleration responses. A head surrogate filled with a hydrogel brain model and a CSF-like medium was subjected to free-fall impacts recorded with an accelerometer, and intracranial pressures were measured at the coup (site of impact) and the contrecoup (opposite of impact). Results revealed that the contrecoup experienced significantly higher peak pressures, reaching 4.3 MPa at 544g, primarily due to cavitation. The coup displayed lower pressures, reaching 0.3 MPa at 550g. Strain analysis showed that the contrecoup exhibited the highest minimum principal strain (ϵmin), indicating greater susceptibility to compression and damage. A linear relationship between impact acceleration (a) and peak pressure (P) was observed in the coup (P = 0.0006a, R2 = 0.97) and the contrecoup (P = 0.0054a, R2 = 0.91), with more variability demonstrated in the contrecoup due to inconsistent formation and growth of cavitation bubbles. These findings suggest that cavitation plays a crucial role in TBI and helps localize damage. Understanding CSF cavitation may support protective technologies and pressure management strategies aimed at reducing injury progression, potentially lowering the risk of neurodegenerative conditions following TBI.

title: Causes and Consequences of Representational Similarity in Machine Learning Models
abstract: Numerous works have noted similarities in how machine learning models represent the world, even across modalities. Although much effort has been devoted to uncovering properties and metrics on which these models align, surprisingly little work has explored causes of this similarity. To advance this line of inquiry, this work explores how two factors—dataset overlap and task overlap—influence downstream model similarity. We evaluate the effects of both factors through experiments across model sizes and modalities, from small classifiers to large language models. We find that dataset and task overlap are positively associated with higher representational similarity across many of our settings, with clear evidence in vision/language classification and weaker trends in language generation experiments. Finally, we consider downstream consequences of representational similarity, showing that greater similarity is associated with increased vulnerability to transferable adversarial attacks in vision models.

title: CausalProfiler: Generating Synthetic Benchmarks for Rigorous and Transparent Evaluation of Causal Machine Learning
abstract: Causal machine learning aims to answer "what if" questions using machine learning algorithms, making it a promising tool for high-stakes decision-making. Yet, empirical evaluation practices remain limited. Existing benchmarks often rely on a handful of hand-crafted or semi-synthetic datasets, leading to brittle, non-generalizable conclusions. To bridge this gap, we introduce CausalProfiler, a synthetic benchmark generator for causal machine learning methods. Based on a set of explicit design choices about the class of causal models, queries, and data considered, CausalProfiler randomly samples causal models, data, queries, and ground truths constituting the synthetic causal benchmarks. In this way, causal machine learning can be rigorously and transparently evaluated under a variety of conditions. This work offers the first random generator of synthetic causal benchmarks with coverage guarantees and transparent assumptions operating on the three levels of causal reasoning: observation, intervention, and counterfactual. We demonstrate its utility by evaluating several state-of-the-art methods under diverse conditions and assumptions, both in and out of the identification regime, illustrating the types of analyses and insights CausalProfiler enables.

title: Cardio-mmFlow: A Gaussian-Prior-Free Physics-Informed Flow Matching Framework for Electrocardiogram to mmWave Radar Synthesis
abstract: Continuous ECG monitoring is clinically valuable, but scaling it beyond electrodes to comfortable long-term use motivates contactless mmWave sensing. In practice, mmWave-to-ECG reconstruction is severely constrained by the scarcity of high-quality synchronized recordings. Therefore, we propose \textbf{Cardio-mmFlow}, a Gaussian-prior-free physics-informed flow matching framework that synthesizes mmWave radar signals from clinical ECG. It learns a direct transport trajectory between the latent manifolds of ECG and radar. Considering subject-dependent propagation differences, we incorporate a simplified mass--spring--damper inspired modulation and inject it into the flow dynamics via feature-wise linear modulation for personalization. Extensive experiments show that our system generates high fidelity radar data in both signal and latent domains. It significantly improves zero-shot downstream mmWave to ECG task, and enable Atrial Fibrillation classification with synthetic data. Further analyses evaluate the model interpretability.

title: CPRISP: an interpretable deep learning framework predicting circRNA-RBP interactions and guiding therapeutic discovery in neurodegeneration
abstract: Abstract Circular RNAs regulate gene expression through interactions with ribonucleic acid binding proteins, but their binding sites remain difficult to predict across proteins and cellular contexts. Existing methods often focus on transcript features while making limited use of protein-specific information and structural context. Here, we show that an integrated deep learning framework combining circular transcript sequence composition, physicochemical properties, secondary structure, pretrained representations and protein features improves interaction-site prediction across 37 benchmark datasets and generalizes across cell lines; model interpretation recovers conserved single-stranded sequence patterns, while analyses of proteins linked to Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis identify recurrent pathways involving nucleocytoplasmic transport, lysosomal signaling and guanosine triphosphatase activity and prioritize compounds for experimental follow-up, supporting accurate and interpretable mapping of circular ribonucleic acid protein interactions without implying therapeutic efficacy.

title: COMPOL: A Unified Neural Operator Framework for Scalable Multi-Physics Simulations
abstract: Multi-physics simulations play an essential role in accurately modeling complex interactions across diverse scientific and engineering domains. Although neural operators, especially the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO), have significantly improved computational efficiency, they often fail to effectively capture intricate correlations inherent in coupled physical processes. To address this limitation, we introduce COMPOL, a novel coupled multi-physics operator learning framework. COMPOL extends conventional operator architectures by incorporating sophisticated recurrent and attention-based aggregation mechanisms, effectively modeling interdependencies among interacting physical processes within latent feature spaces. Our approach is architecture-agnostic and seamlessly integrates into various neural operator frameworks that involve latent space transformations. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks—including biological reaction-diffusion systems, pattern-forming chemical reactions, multiphase geological flows, and thermo-hydro-mechanical processes — demonstrate that COMPOL consistently achieves superior predictive accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods.

title: CINOC: Cardinality-Invariant Neural Operator Policies for Scalable PDE Control
abstract: Controlling partial differential equations (PDEs) with learning-based policies remains fundamentally limited by fixed-dimensional representations: policies trained for a specific sensor, actuator, or agent configuration typically fail when the configuration changes. This limitation is particularly severe in multi-agent PDE control, where policies do not scale across population sizes without retraining. We address this challenge by introducing **C**ardinality **I**nvariant **N**eural **O**perator **C**ontrol (**CINOC**), reformulating PDE control as an operator learning problem that maps state fields to continuous control functions and trains them end-to-end through differentiable PDE solvers, yielding policies that naturally adapt to varying sensor and actuator configurations. Remarkably, CINOC policies trained on small swarms exhibit cardinality invariance, allowing for zero-shot transfer to significantly larger populations as well as robustness to partial agent failure. This scalability arises from agents sharing a common policy and coordinating through their physical environment, which produces an emergent self-normalization effect. To explain this phenomenon, we provide a theorem grounded in mean-field theory demonstrating that policy gradients computed from finite-agent systems converge to those of a continuous control limit. Empirically, we validate CINOC on tracking, stabilization, and density transport across linear, nonlinear, chaotic, and turbulent PDEs.

title: CATF: A Manager-Worker Framework for Context-Aware Time-Series Forecasting
abstract: We study context-aware time-series forecasting, in which a single target variable is predicted from its own history and a set of contextual variables, such as weather and calendar information. As the context becomes more diverse, a single model struggles to capture all of its regimes, while ensemble learning and Mixture-of-Experts approaches rely on manual data partitioning or soft routing, which increases the inference cost and hinders interpretability. We propose CATF, a Context-Aware Time-Series Forecasting framework built on a Manager-Worker architecture: a Transformer-based Manager routes each input to a single Worker based on the context, using hard routing during both training and inference. The Workers thus specialize without manual data partitioning, and any single-model forecaster can serve as a Worker. On five context-rich datasets, four horizons, and two normalization schemes, CATF improves over its standalone counterpart in 162 of 200 comparisons, the best CATF-enhanced model outperforms the best standalone baseline in 19 of 20 settings, and it outperforms the zero-shot Time-MoE foundation model in 15 of 20 settings. A case study on bike-sharing data shows that the Manager routes inputs by the calendar and that each Worker specializes in a different weekly pattern.

title: C-WFDM: A ControlNet-Guided Wavelet-Fusion Diffusion Model for Multimodal Brain MRI Completion
abstract: Multimodal brain MRI provides complementary anatomical, tissue, and pathological information to support downstream artificial intelligence (AI) applications. However, modality availability is uneven across public and pooled neuroimaging datasets: T1-weighted (T1w) MRI is widely represented, T2-weighted (T2w) and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) MRI are less consistently available, and gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted (T1Gd) MRI is relatively scarce. Pooled datasets therefore contain participants with different combinations of acquired MRI contrasts, reflecting variation in the study designs, acquisition protocols, and clinical or research objectives of the contributing studies. Many missing-modality benchmarks simulate incomplete MRI by withholding contrasts from complete four-modality cases, which may not represent the observed availability patterns in pooled datasets. To address this gap, we introduce C-WFDM, a ControlNet extension of our Wavelet-Fusion Diffusion Model (WFDM), for subject-specific missing-modality completion. C-WFDM is built on an earlier BrainScape snapshot comprising 157 public MRI datasets and 45,880 preprocessed scans. The pretrained WFDM backbone retains target-modality and metadata conditioning, while target-specific ControlNet adapters use MRI contrasts from the same participant to guide synthesis. C-WFDM synthesizes T2w from T1w, FLAIR from T1w and T2w, and T1Gd from T1w, T2w, and FLAIR. Acquired conditioning contrasts are used when available, and generated intermediate contrasts are used only when required. We compare C-WFDM with ALDM, cWDM, and Pix2Pix using paired structural similarity index (SSIM), peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), and mean absolute error (MAE). In the BrainScape completion experiment, C-WFDM achieves the best T2w and FLAIR results among the evaluated models, with SSIM values of 0.9232 and 0.8904, respectively.

title: Bypass transition beneath internal solitary waves in turbulent boundary layers
abstract: Process-based studies of the transition to turbulence beneath internal solitary waves (ISWs) have typically assumed a laminar bottom boundary layer (BBL) and two-dimensional flow. In natural environments, however, ISWs often propagate over turbulent three-dimensional BBLs. Here, we perform three-dimensional high-resolution spectral numerical simulations of periodic ISWs of depression at momentum-thickness Reynolds numbers representative of laboratory ( upper R e Subscript upper I upper S upper W Baseline equals 300 R e I S W = 300 $Re_{ISW}=300$ ) and lake ( upper R e Subscript upper I upper S upper W Baseline equals 900 R e I S W = 900 $Re_{ISW}=900$ ) scale conditions to examine how ambient turbulence modifies the transition to turbulence beneath ISWs. When the ambient flow is laminar, this transition is governed by a modal instability. At upper R e Subscript upper I upper S upper W Baseline equals 300 R e I S W = 300 $Re_{ISW}=300$ , the instability generates localised vortices that subsequently break down, while at upper R e Subscript upper I upper S upper W Baseline equals 900 R e I S W = 900 $Re_{ISW}=900$ it produces sustained vortex shedding and a turbulent wake in the lee of the wave. In contrast, when the ambient flow is turbulent, the modal pathway is bypassed. Free-stream turbulence excites near-wall streamwise streaks (Klebanoff modes) beneath the front shoulder of the wave, which amplify, undergo secondary instability and break down into turbulent bursts. The resulting turbulence develops upstream of the modal-instability region. With increasing Reynolds number and stronger ambient turbulence, the onset of turbulence shifts progressively toward the ISW trough. These results show that ambient turbulence triggers a bypass mechanism fundamentally different from the modal-instability-driven transition in laminar environments. By suppressing the modal instability and shifting turbulence generation closer to the wave trough, bypass transition provides an explanation for field observations that cannot be reconciled with laminar-transition models. Accurate prediction of near-bed turbulence and sediment transport in natural environments therefore requires accounting for bypass transition.

title: Bridging Semantics and Structure: A Theoretically Grounded Framework for Link Prediction on TAGs
abstract: Link prediction on text-attributed graphs (TAGs) is a fundamental problem with applications in knowledge discovery, recommendation and beyond. Recent progress has highlighted the promise of combining Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with Language Models (LMs) in order to leverage the complementary structural and semantic signals. However, due to the distinct inductive biases of GNNs and LMs, the design of an optimal fusion strategy remains an open research question. In this work, we present Bridge-LP, an intuitive, simple, efficient and theoretically grounded framework that unifies graph and language representations. It is built around three theoretically-justified design components: (D1) jumping connection of textual proximity, which enables robust LM training; (D2) compressed embedding, which encodes neighborhood information long exploited by classical link prediction heuristics, thereby enriching structural signals in a learnable way; and (D3) cache embedding training strategy, which reduces computational complexity. Together, these mechanisms establish an end-to-end cross-modal framework that scales to large graphs while capturing richer graph-text interactions. We conduct an extensive empirical evaluation, comparing against 40 existing models across 9 diverse datasets. Experiments show that Bridge-LP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, delivering up to a 43.06% improvement in Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) and setting a new benchmark for language-graph integration.

title: Boosted Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Solving Homogeneous and Non-Homogeneous Lane-Emden Type Equations
abstract: The Lane-Emden Equation is a class of nonlinear differential equations commonly used to model phenomena in astrophysics and mathematical physics, such as stellar structure and thermal behavior in polytropic gas spheres. This study presents a novel hybrid framework that integrates Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) with boosting methods to enhance the accuracy and robustness of solutions for Lane-Emden type differential equations. Standard PINNs leverage physical laws encoded within the loss function, but their predictive performance can be constrained by optimization challenges and approximation errors. To address this, we introduce a post-processing boosting stage where the residual errors from the PINN prediction are modeled using some regression algorithms - including LightGBM, Random Forest, XGBoost, and Support Vector Regression (SVR). The outputs from these boosted models are aggregated to generate a corrected, high-fidelity prediction. The proposed methodology is systematically validated through quantitative metrics and comparative analysis against the standard PINN baseline. The results demonstrate that the boosted PINN framework significantly reduces prediction error, and improves generalization, offering a powerful and flexible approach for solving scientific and engineering problems governed by differential equations.

title: Black Hole Love Numbers with Physics-Informed Neural Networks
abstract: We develop and validate a physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework for computing the tidal Love numbers of black holes directly from their perturbation equations. We consider static perturbations of the Kerr black hole, whose exact hypergeometric solutions provide a controlled benchmark for both the numerical solver and the extraction of the physical response. The framework combines exact enforcement of the horizon boundary conditions with an $H^2$-Sobolev loss that incorporates derivatives of the differential-equation residual. The Love number is then obtained by extracting the asymptotic coefficients of the learned solution, without using the analytic connection formula. Across the tested scalar, vector, and tensor perturbations, the method recovers the finite dissipative response with relative errors below $10^{-5}$. Controlled comparisons show that the higher-derivative loss terms improve solution accuracy by orders of magnitude, while independent tests of the extraction procedure distinguish solver errors from errors in recovering the response coefficients. The conservative response, which vanishes analytically, is constrained by the numerical error floor. These results demonstrate that PINNs can accurately compute black-hole tidal response and establish a validated framework for future extensions to frequency-dependent and non-separable perturbation problems.

title: BhopalMLS: A LiDAR Dataset for Semantic Scene Understanding in Heterogeneous Urban Environments
abstract: We introduce BhopalMLS, a large-scale Mobile Laser Scanning (MLS) dataset from a dense, heterogeneous urban environment in Bhopal, India, with mixed traffic, informal structures, and narrow unplanned streets. It spans approximately 10 km of road corridors with over 1.2 billion points and 19,518 annotated instances across 62 fine-grained static categories, grouped into 12-class and 21-class benchmark taxonomies; 6 optional moving-class subclasses support dynamic-object analysis. Existing 3D datasets, collected in well-planned cities, are structurally more uniform than such unplanned settings, and lack their subtype diversity. On semantic and instance segmentation at both granularities, fine-tuned foundation models surpass supervised baselines: Utonia(L) reaches 71.28% mIoU (vs. PTv3's 68.04% from scratch) and 44.07% mAP50 on the 12-class benchmark. Cross-region experiments against four established datasets (Ke-MLS, Toronto-3D, Paris-Lille-3D, SemanticKITTI) reveal a consistent asymmetric transferability: models trained on BhopalMLS transfer better than the reverse on every pair, for both Utonia(L) and Concerto(L) (mean 21.5, up to 36 mIoU points), holding even when the target is denser. Factor-controlled retraining at a fixed label budget, repeated on both models, attributes this to the coverage of BhopalMLS's subtype inventory rather than to dataset size or corridor geometry: collapsing each class to a single subtype costs 13.0 and 13.3 mIoU points for Utonia(L) and Concerto(L). BhopalMLS therefore offers a testbed for 3D perception beyond well-planned cities. Data and an interactive viewer are at https://geoai4cities.github.io/bhopalmls.

title: Beyond Foundation Models: PFN Priors Improve Tabular Hyperparameter Optimization
abstract: Synthetic priors have so far served one purpose: pretraining tabular foundation models. We ask whether the same priors can improve conventional tabular models, which are trained from scratch on each dataset. We propose PriorTune, a method that meta-tunes hyperparameter configurations on synthetic tasks alone. Offline, for a given model, we fit a pool of configurations on datasets sampled from a published PFN prior and greedily select the subset with the highest winrate over the random baseline. Online, a new dataset fits only the selected configurations, so the gain comes at no extra cost. Empirically, we observe that scaling both the number of configurations and synthetic datasets has an equal scaling effect on the performance of the final subset of configurations, which we also explain theoretically. On the full BeyondArena benchmark, LightGBM with TabPrep features with our configurations ranks above TabPFN-3 and RealMLP, while being much more efficient at inference. Overall, our results establish existing PFN priors as a scalable source of meta-training data for hyperparameter selection for non-foundational tabular models.

title: Benchmarking the Scientific Mind: A Pathology-Derived Biomedical VQA Benchmark for Complex Scientific Reasoning
abstract: Despite progress of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in biomedical visual question answering (VQA), existing benchmarks provide limited assessment of their scientific reasoning capabilities. Most datasets adopt single-image question construction and outcome-oriented evaluation, where correctness is judged by answer plausibility rather than alignment with experimental evidence. Such formulations fail to capture the evidence-constrained, multi-step nature of biomedical reasoning, and obscure whether models can derive conclusions through causal interpretation of experimental observations. To address these critical gaps in reasoning evaluation, we propose a principled benchmark construction framework that reconstructs scientific reasoning paths directly from biomedical literature. By jointly modeling clusters of experimentally related images together with their captions and context, the framework generates tightly coupled question–reasoning–answer triples that require multi-image integration and explicit evidence-driven inference. Based on this framework, we introduce SORBE (Scientific Observation & Reasoning for Biomedical Evaluation), a large-scale multi-image pathology-derived biomedical VQA benchmark designed to evaluate evidence alignment and multi-step experimental reasoning. Under a process-oriented evaluation metric, state-of-the-art biomedical-specialized MLLMs exhibit substantial performance degradation, revealing systematic limitations in evidence grounding and causal reasoning that are not reflected by existing benchmarks. Data and code are available at: https://github.com/UniverseOfUniverse/SORBE.git.

title: Benchmarking Physics-Informed Time-Series Models for Operational Global Station Weather Forecasting
abstract: The development of Time-Series Forecasting (TSF) models is often constrained by the lack of comprehensive datasets, especially in Global Station Weather Forecasting (GSWF), where existing datasets are small, temporally short, and spatially sparse. To address this, we introduce WEATHER-5K, a large-scale observational weather dataset that better reflects real-world conditions and supports improved model training and evaluation. While recent TSF methods perform well on benchmarks, they still lag behind operational Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) systems in capturing complex weather dynamics and extreme events. We propose PhysicsFormer, a physics-informed forecasting model that combines a dynamic core with a Transformer residual to predict future weather states. Physical consistency is enforced via pressure–wind alignment and energy-aware smoothness losses, ensuring plausible dynamics while capturing complex temporal patterns. We benchmark PhysicsFormer and other TSF models against operational systems across several weather variables, extreme event prediction, and model complexity, providing a comprehensive assessment of the gap between academic TSF models and operational forecasting. The dataset and benchmark implementation are available at: https://github.com/taohan10200/WEATHER-5K.

title: Benchmarking Physical Reasoning of Video Generative Models with Real Physical Experiments
abstract: Recent advances in image and video generation raise hopes that these models possess world modeling capabilities—the ability to generate realistic, physically plausible videos. This could revolutionize applications in robotics, autonomous driving, and scientific simulation. However, before treating these models as world models, we must ask: Do they adhere to physical laws? Current evaluation methods rely on subjective judgments or trajectory matching, limiting their usage for physical reasoning estimation, where many generations could be physically plausible. Thus, we introduce **Morpheus**, a new benchmark for evaluating video generation models on physical reasoning. It features 130 real-world videos capturing physical phenomena, guided by conservation laws. Using those as conditioning for video generation, we assess physical plausibility using physics-informed metrics evaluated with respect to infallible conservation laws known per physical setting, leveraging advances in physics-informed neural networks and vision-language foundation models. % Since artificial generations lack ground truth, we assess physical plausibility using physics-informed metrics evaluated with respect to infallible conservation laws known per physical setting, leveraging advances in physics-informed neural networks and vision-language foundation models. Our findings reveal that even with advanced prompting and video conditioning, current models struggle to encode physical principles despite generating aesthetically pleasing videos.

title: Behind Video Generation: Observations and Insights on Multimodal Understanding from Kling
abstract: Video generation has progressed from isolated clips to coherent short-form audiovisual sequences, and the bottleneck is shifting from rendering to semantic control. This report summarizes the observations and insights on multimodal understanding gained from successive generations of Kling. We argue that generation quality is the projection of multimodal understanding through the entire data--conditioning--alignment--evaluation chain, and we examine this chain module by module. Kling-MLLM, a shared multimodal foundation model that unifies image, video, audio, synchronized audio--video, and interleaved inputs, is specialized for each downstream module. Because a DiT is trained on far fewer training samples than a language model, we treat captioning as a semantic contract that maximizes description density, and extend it to reference-grounded captioning that makes reference bindings explicit. Prompt enhancement translates user intent into this caption distribution: basic PE is derived from captions of compelling videos and refined with text-level and generator-in-the-loop reinforcement learning, while agentic PE refines the story and retrieves compelling examples. We show that a reliable text encoder comes from perceptual training rather than from stronger language ability, and that candidates can be screened from text alone before end-to-end training. Reward modeling pairs a general reward model for explainable, localized critiques with a decision reward model for fast multidimensional scoring, treating perceptual bandwidth as a first-class design parameter. Finally, we review task-specific automatic evaluation, focusing on protocols that expose scoring shortcuts and help trace failures to their upstream source. We hope these lessons offer practical guidance for building the understanding stack behind controllable video generation.

title: Backstress-dominated regimes of fluid-driven fractures in poroelastic media: a simplified asymptotic framework
abstract: This paper examines how poroelastic backstress induced by fluid leak-off modifies the asymptotic propagation regimes of fluid-driven fractures. We consider a simplified theoretical framework in which the diffusion zone remains small relative to the fracture size, so that Carter-type leak-off can be coupled consistently with one-dimensional fracture models. Within this setting, leak-off-induced pore-pressure diffusion generates a backstress that acts against fracture-opening and alters the classical regime structure. Three typical geometries are studied: plane strain; radial; constant-height fractures. For each geometry, we derive the corresponding backstress-dominated self-similar limit, referred to as the upper B B $B$ -vertex, and incorporate it into the classical parametric space of hydraulic fracture propagation. The analysis shows that, when poroelastic effects are sufficiently strong, the classical leak-off-dominated asymptotic regimes may cease to exist and the fracture evolves instead towards the backstress-dominated state. Transition solutions connecting the classical limiting regimes to the upper B B $B$ -vertex are also obtained. The results extend the standard asymptotic classification of hydraulic fractures by identifying a distinct regime controlled by poroelastic backstress. They also provide a simple framework for assessing when backstress is expected to play a leading role in fluid-driven fracture propagation across different geometries and scales.

title: BALLAST: Bayesian Active Learning with Look-ahead Amendment for Sea-drifter Trajectories under Spatio-Temporal Vector Fields
abstract: We introduce a formal active learning methodology for guiding the placement of Lagrangian observers to infer time-dependent vector fields -- a key task in oceanography, marine science, and ocean engineering -- using a physics-informed spatio-temporal Gaussian process surrogate model. The majority of existing placement campaigns either follow standard `space-filling' designs or relatively ad-hoc expert opinions. A key challenge to applying principled active learning in this setting is that Lagrangian observers are continuously advected through the vector field, so they make measurements at different locations and times. It is, therefore, important to consider the likely future trajectories of placed observers to account for the utility of candidate placement locations. To this end, we present BALLAST: Bayesian Active Learning with Look-ahead Amendment for Sea-drifter Trajectories. We observe noticeable benefits of BALLAST-aided sequential observer placement strategies on both synthetic and high-fidelity ocean current models. In addition, we developed a novel GP inference method -- the Vanilla SPDE Exchange (VaSE) -- to boost the GP posterior sampling efficiency, which is also of independent interest.

title: Axiomatic Atlas: A Prescriptive Framework for Neural Architecture Design
abstract: Neural architecture design lacks first principles: innovations are discovered empirically and justified post-hoc, with no systematic way to diagnose *why* an architecture fails or derive *what* repair will succeed. We introduce the *Axiomatic Atlas*, encoding requirements as composable axioms over graph connectivity, operator contracts, numerical stability, and information preservation. Given an operator library and wiring conventions, the Atlas constructs certificates lower-bounding output variation via min-cut analysis and diagnoses failures by locating axiom violations. Crucially, the framework is prescriptive: each violation implies a targeted repair, reducing architecture design to constraint satisfaction. We prove variation bounds under exact and finite-precision arithmetic, enabling modular verification across transformers, MoEs, SSMs, and GNNs. Four Atlas-derived interventions validate the approach: +46 percentage points on GNN bottlenecks, $3\times$ robustness to MoE quantization, 83\% gap closure with adaptive expert budgets, and 0\%$\to$100\% retrieval via orthogonal keys---each against matched negative controls.

title: AutoFigure: Generating and Refining Publication-Ready Scientific Illustrations
abstract: High-quality scientific illustrations are crucial for effectively communicating complex scientific and technical concepts, yet their manual creation remains a well-recognized bottleneck in both academia and industry. We present FigureBench, the first large-scale benchmark for generating scientific illustrations from long-form scientific texts. It contains 3,300 high-quality scientific text–figure pairs, covering diverse text-to-illustration tasks from scientific papers, surveys, blogs, and textbooks. Moreover, we propose AutoFigure, an agentic framework that automatically generates high-quality scientific illustrations based on long-form scientific text. Specifically, before rendering the final result, AutoFigure engages in extensive thinking, recombination, and validation to produce a layout that is both structurally sound and aesthetically refined, outputting a scientific illustration that achieves both structural completeness and aesthetic appeal. Leveraging the high-quality data from FigureBench, we conduct extensive experiments to test the performance of AutoFigure against various baseline methods. The results demonstrate that Autofigure consistently surpasses all baseline methods, producing publication-ready scientific illustrations.

title: AutoBalance: An Automatic Balancing Framework for Training Physics-Informed Neural Networks
abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) provide a powerful and general framework for solving Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) by embedding physical laws into loss functions. However, training PINNs is notoriously difficult due to the need to balance multiple loss terms, such as PDE residuals and boundary conditions, which often have conflicting objectives and vastly different curvatures. Existing methods address this issue by manipulating gradients before optimization (a "pre-combine" strategy). We argue that this approach is fundamentally limited, as forcing a single optimizer to process gradients from spectrally heterogeneous loss landscapes disrupts its internal preconditioning. In this work, we introduce AutoBalance, a novel "post-combine" training paradigm. AutoBalance assigns an independent adaptive optimizer to each loss component and aggregates the resulting preconditioned updates afterwards. Extensive experiments on challenging PDE benchmarks show that AutoBalance consistently outperforms existing frameworks, achieving significant reductions in solution error, as measured by both the MSE and $L^{\infty}$ norms. Moreover, AutoBalance is orthogonal to and complementary with other popular PINN methodologies, amplifying their effectiveness on demanding benchmarks.

title: Atom-Wise Allocation of Message-Passing Scale for Molecular Property Prediction
abstract: Molecular properties depend on chemical structure at different ranges, from local polar groups governing solvation to extended substructures shaping bioactivity, yet graph neural networks usually fix one propagation scale for every atom. We present PRISM (Per-atom Routing over Intermediate States of Message Passing), in which each atom's encoded features produce a bounded scalar that positions a unimodal distribution over retained message-passing states and matching circular-fingerprint radii. Because one coordinate translates the whole profile, allocated depth responds to the routing scalar in closed form: at fixed temperature it is nondecreasing, its sensitivity scales with the profile variance, and it saturates in the clipped regions. Beyond providing closed-form analyzability, this constrained one-parameter profile matches or significantly outperforms parameter-matched, unconstrained node-wise gates and Jumping Knowledge attention. Under scaffold partitions with equal tuning budgets against eight graph, fingerprint, and geometric baselines, PRISM trained from scratch without three-dimensional coordinates achieves the lowest mean error on aqueous solubility and hydration free energy and strong accuracy on BACE and BBBP. As a general layer-combination rule, PRISM transfers directly to GCN, GIN, and GAT backbones, reducing hydration free energy error by up to 29% relative to last-layer readout. Applied to a pre-trained GIN, it improves on last-layer readout on four of six endpoints and gives the lowest lipophilicity error overall. In trained models, allocated depth differs systematically between atom types in a task-dependent way, and permuting profiles among a molecule's atoms raises prediction error on several endpoints, so the rule acts as a learned counterpart of atom typing.

title: Asynchronous Robot Policies
abstract: Scaling vision-language foundation models has significantly advanced generalist robot manipulation, but the increased model scale introduces computational latency that degrades real-time physical reactivity. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures execute high-level semantic reasoning and action ex- ecution sequentially within the primary control loop, creating a fundamental tension between semantic-reasoning capability and robot agility. To address this, we propose Asynchronous Robot Policy (ARP), an architectural framework that decouples semantic reasoning from low-level action generation using asynchronous processes operating at independent frequencies. In ARP, a high-capacity Vision-Language Model (VLM) asynchronously updates a semantic memory at low fre- quency, while a lightweight Vision-Action Expert, conditioned on this semantic memory, generates robot actions at a much higher control frequency. Such a formulation, enables having a fast perception-action loop without compromising on the semantic capability. To overcome asynchronous memory staleness, ARP trains the vision-action expert on the semantic staleness and execution delay, with temporally mismatched observation across processes. On Franka manipulation tasks, ARP achieves an 18% higher success rate and 20% less time need for execution in quasi-static setups, while 3-5 times baseline performance in dynamic simulation environments. Furthermore, ARP enables operating the VLM at 10 times lower than its nominal frequency with no significant performance loss making it much more efficient than the baseline. These results highlight the architectural advantages of modeling robot policies as asynchronous processes, enabling real-world reactive deployment without sacrificing the scale of foundation models.

title: Ascend-SpMM: Accelerating Sparse Matrix-Dense Matrix Multiplication on Ascend NPUs
abstract: Sparse Matrix-Dense Matrix Multiplication (SpMM) is a fundamental kernel in graph neural networks and scientific computing, yet its optimization on Ascend NPUs remains largely unexplored. The physically decoupled Cube/Vector architecture and single-threaded scalar instruction dispatch of modern NPUs introduce unique challenges. We present Ascend-SpMM, a novel and systematic framework tailored to the physically decoupled architecture of Ascend NPUs.We introduce a memory-centric cost model that quantifies hardware affinity and guides a conflict-bounded, densityaware task-mapping strategy. The strategy maps dense regions to the high-throughput Cube path and sparse residuals to the flexible Vector path, with a theoretical bound on cross-processor conflicts. To execute these workloads with high efficiency, we further develop highly customized sub-kernels. These kernels leverage hierarchy-aware pipelining and round-robin ring buffer-based implicit synchronization to effectively mask memory latency and reduce instruction pipeline stalls. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Ascend-SpMM achieves a geometric-mean speedup of 12.70-20.55X over the strongest evaluated NPU baseline for each matrix, accelerates end-to-end GNN training by up to 6.8X, and delivers performance competitive with state-of-the-art GPU implementations. The source code of Ascend-SpMM is publicly available at https://github.com/IDMG-Lab/Ascend-SpMM.

title: ArtifactLinker: Linking Scientific Artifacts for Automatic SOTA Discovery
abstract: Scientific artifacts, such as models and benchmarks, are the foundation of machine learning research. With the rapid growth of repositories like HuggingFace, researchers now have access to millions of high-quality artifacts contributed by different researchers, yet the challenge remains: how can we automatically discover the state-of-the-art (SOTA) model for a given benchmark, fully leveraging existing scientific artifacts? We address this task, abbreviated as automatic SOTA discovery, by first modeling HuggingFace as an artifact graph, where nodes represent models or benchmarks and edges capture their relationships, labeled with evaluation results. Within this graph, we formulate the automatic SOTA discovery as the process of identifying new unobserved links with high potential performance that could advance future research. To enable scalable and efficient discovery of SOTA artifact links, we propose ArtifactLinker, a two-stage framework for automatic SOTA discovery: (1) prediction, which identifies promising links with Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) or graph-augmented LLMs, and (2) verification, which validates promising predicted links through reproducible and automatic coding experiments and agents. To evaluate ArtifactLinker, we further propose ArtifactBench, collecting 1,372 models and 308 benchmarks for systematically measuring prediction and verification performance and helping to develop new SOTA discovery agents. Our key results indicate that the graph-based prediction module in ArtifactLinker is effective in prediction. Moreover, an automatic verification pipeline in ArtifactLinker can verify that the identified promising links indeed achieve high performance on existing benchmarks in a fully automatic way.
